A tornado tracked north at 20 mph near Interstate 29 destroying at least one farmyard and tossing vehicles.  At 315 PM CDT the tornado ripped through a farmyard seven miles north of Beresford destroying a large barn, silo, and numerous outbuildings, and killing 15 hogs.  Also lost were 40 tons of hay and 1200 bales of straw.  The owner of the farm was driving a tractor when one of at least two tornadoes dipped down, overturning the 11,000 lb. tractor and loader. The semi was estimated to be a total loss.  A young boy was injured when he was struck by a car on Interstate 29 while seeking shelter under an overpass. The new Mill Avenue Bridge was washed away by the raging Salt River.  A large landfill in Mesa was washed away.  The Gillespie Dam west of Phoenix was damaged as high water spread throughout low-lying areas.  Many roads closed and motorists stranded by flooded dips and washes.  Phoenix alone sustained at least $4.2 million in damages from this prolonged period of heavy rains.  This January was the wettest January on record with 5.22 inches at the airport.  It was also the 4th all- time wettest month.  Total rainfall for both December and January was 8.30 inches; this was the greatest ever for any two consecutive months. Arizona experienced its worst flooding in a decade as record rainfall and associated flooding forced many from homes and disrupted business.  The Red Cross reported 678 dwellings destroyed or damaged.  Early estimates of damage were at least $56 million statewide.  A Presidential Federal Disaster Declaration was requested and signed by the President on January 19th. Several storm systems affected the state before the major storm arrived during the night of January 7-8.  Significant precipitation of two to three inches were reported in a few sites between Phoenix and the Mogollon Rim.  Moist low-level flow was forced upward and resulted in heavy rain and snow in the highest elevations.  Periods of heavy rainfall resulted from the interaction of dynamic forcing and convective instability.  The most significant flash flood events occurred when convective rains fell on watersheds already saturated from earlier rainfall.  Another factor contributing to the unusually high runoffs and associated flooding was snow melt.  The snow level during the 6th to the 8th rose to about 8,500 feet, several thousand feet above typical snow levels.  In summary, the combination of a northward-displaced subtropical jet, with its abundant moisture supply and associated disturbances, and a southward-displaced polar jet, with its storm track, led to the abnormally wet period from just after Christmas to mid-January.

A stationary front was located across Iowa once again.  It extended from near Omaha to just south of Des Moines to near the Quad Cities. Urban flooding was reported in Webster County, but was not of the magnitude of many of the flooding events that occurred throughout the summer.

Severe thunderstorms developed in northeast Oklahoma ahead of a cold front during the late afternoon of April 24th and moved across eastern and portions of eastern Oklahoma during the night.  The thunderstorms spawned 8 tornadoes, and produced hail to baseball-size and damaging straight line winds. The first two tornadoes of the day were the most destructive.  The  first tornado touched down in East Tulsa near 6th Street and 135th East Avenue at 1750 CST.  This tornado moved northeast for about a mile before entering Rogers County at 1753 CST.  There, a truck stop near Interstate 44 and 161st East Avenue took a direct hit from the tornado.  Numerous tractor- trailers and cars were destroyed in the vicinity of the truck stop.  Six people were killed at or near the truck stop.  The tornado then continued northeast into Catoosa where several residential neighborhoods and the Colonial Port Mobile Home Park received heavy damage.  The 7th and final fatality associated with this tornado occurred at the mobile home park.  The tornado dissipated at 1803 CST 1 mile west of State Highway 66 north of Catoosa.  This F4 tornado traveled 5.5 miles and was 250 yards wide.  (M70P)(M39V)(F39V)(F8V)(M33V)(M35O)(F77M) A second tornado formed at 1757 CST near the truck stop at Interstate 44 and 161st East Avenue and moved east northeast.  This tornado also caused heavy damage to Catoosa, but resulted in no additional fatalities.  The tornado lifted at 1815 CST 1.5 miles north of State Highway 412 to the east of Catoosa.  This F3 tornado traveled 8 miles and was 250 yards wide.  The two tornadoes injured about 130 people, and damaged or destroyed 70% of the businesses in Catoosa.  Damage estimates for Catoosa schools was estimated at $8 to $10 million, with the high school sustaining the brunt of the damage.  Total damage caused by the tornadoes has been estimated at over $100 million.  This thunderstorm also produced a microburst which destroyed a church at 15th Street and Memorial Drive in Tulsa, and damaged several other Tulsa businesses.  Straight line winds also caused damage to homes and destroyed two mobile homes in Wagoner County.  In all, approximately 858 dwellings were affected by the storms.  Preliminary figures by county are as follows: Tulsa County - 116 homes were damaged, 17 mobile homes were damaged, 3 businesses were destroyed, 40 businesses were damaged, 1 public building was destroyed, 2 public buildings were damaged, 1 church building was destroyed, and 5 church buildings were damaged; Rogers County - 163 homes were destroyed, 147 homes were damaged, 100 mobile homes were destroyed, 41 rental units were damaged or destroyed, 49 businesses were damaged or destroyed, and 15 public buildings were damaged or destroyed; Wagoner County - 111 homes were damaged and 2 mobile homes were destroyed. The third tornado touched down at 1846 CST, 4 miles west of Locust Grove in Mayes County and moved east northeast for 4.5 miles before lifting at 1856 CST, 1.5 miles north of Locust Grove.  The tornado destroyed 1 house and 5 mobile homes, and damaged 10 houses and 7 mobile homes.  Several barns and outbuildings were also destroyed.  One minor injury was caused by the tornado.  This F2 tornado caused around $500,000 worth of damage and was 150 yards wide. The 4th and 8th tornadoes were brief F0-tornado with no significant damage reported.  The tornadoes occurred 2 miles west of Rose in Mayes County at 1917CST, near Chance in Adair County at 2015 CST, 4 miles northeast of Centrahoma in Coal County at 2155 CST, near Ashland in Pittsburg County at 2215 CST and 4 miles west of Wapanucka in Johnston County at 2235 CST. Strong thunderstorm winds downed trees and power lines, and destroyed barns and outbuildings at several locations.  Strong straight line winds destroyed a mobile home 2 miles south-southeast of Leach, destroyed a chicken house 3 miles southwest of Leach, damaged barns and gates 10 miles west of Atoka and downed 4 power poles near Idabel.  Large hail was widespread with the storms.  Baseball-size hail fell 10 miles east of Catoosa and 2 miles northwest of Locust Grove.  Golfball-size hail covered the ground along State Highway 412 from 2 miles west of Inola to 1 mile south of Chouteau.  A lightning strike started an oil tank battery fire near Lindsay.

Tornadoes, Thunderstorm Winds, Hail, Storm Surge, Flooding, Beach Erosion, SnowThe "Storm Of The Century" roared across Florida producing a variety of severe and unusual weather conditions for a period of about 18 hours from late Friday the 12th through late afternoon Saturday the 13th.  A severe squall line raced eastward at 50 mph ahead of an intense low producing several tornadoes and strong downbursts as it moved through the state and directly caused seven fatalities.  This was followed by a hitherto unknown  (for the Gulf Coast) winter storm surge of 9 to 12 feet onto the gulf coast in Taylor County, with storm surges and/or tidal and wind driven flooding of 5 to 9 feet elsewhere along the gulf coast of the state and into the lower Keys.  This was followed by a period of 8 to 12 hours of high sustained winds of up to 50 mph with gusts to 70 mph, keeping tides much above normal along the west coast and causing severe beach erosion in many areas.  Total number of fatalities from the storm was 47, including 14 from storm surge and flooding, seven from tornadoes and/or strong downbursts, and four from high winds in the aftermath of the squall line.  Eleven people drowned offshore in the Gulf of Mexico after strong winds swamped or capsized ships  (including seven crewmen from a 200-foot Honduran freighter).  Eleven others died during rescue operations and cleanup activities. Numerous strong to severe thunderstorms developed in southwestern Oklahoma during the afternoon hours on the 29th and moved eastward into central and eastern Oklahoma during the evening and nighttime hours.  Four weak tornadoes occurred in Oklahoma with this outbreak of severe weather.  An F0 tornado occurred 2 miles west of Elk City and knocked down power poles and power lines.  An F0 tornado briefly touched down in an open field in extreme southeast Tillman County 6 miles southeast of Grandfield, with no damage reported.  The third tornado had the longest path of the four.  This tornado traveled along a 5-mile path from 4 miles east of Alex to 3 miles west of Criner.  The tornado was narrowrow (35 yards wide) and produced mainly F0 damage with a small area of F1 damage in McClain County.  The fourth tornado developed after midnight in Lincoln County and moved into Okfuskee County along its 4.5-mile path from two miles southeast of Prague to 2.5 miles west-southwest of Paden.  The tornado was an F1 and averaged 100 yards in width.  The tornado rolled an abandoned bus 75 feet to the east-southeast and lifted a camper trailer 75 feet to the north.  The tornado also tossed an 18-foot horse trailer into a barn, demolishing both structures.  The tornado produced an estimated $250,000 in damage. Large hail also accompanied many of the storms.  Softball-size hail was reported in Texola and near Sayre.  Baseball-size hail fell shortly before 2200 CST and then again after 2300 CST in Waurika.  The large hail in combination with strong winds and flash flooding caused between $250,000 and $500,000 in damage in Waurika.  Numerous other locations in southwest Oklahoma received quarter- to golfball-size hail. Strong winds also caused widespread damage throughout southwest, central, and eastern Oklahoma.  During the evening hours, a very small but intense microburst destroyed a building in Verden.  Damage was estimated at $45,000.  Strong thunderstorm winds near 70 mph blew out windows at several businesses in Frederick and blew a portion of the roof off the Frederick Middle School.  Strong thunderstorm winds blew down a power line near Hammon, and winds estimated at between 70 and 80 mph occurred near Granite.  In Dover, a downburst produced winds estimated at 60 mph which destroyed a mobile home, downed a power pole and some trees and broke off numerous tree limbs up to 10 inches in diameter.  In Okmulgee County, severe thunderstorm winds during the early morning hours of the 30th blew an unoccupied mobile home over 5 miles to the west of Beggs.  Strong winds in Alex broke off tree limbs, downed several power poles, and tore part of a roof off of a house.  High winds from a thunderstorm, severely damaged a sheet metal barn and blew down trees 2 miles south-southeast of Prague.  Winds from severe thunderstorms blew down numerous trees along a path from 2 miles southeast of Prague to 4 miles east of Prague.  Strong winds downed trees 5 miles south of Randlett. Widespread flash flooding was reported with these storms.  High water in Waurika flooded three homes.  One home which was not occupied had about a foot of water flowing through it.  A few other homes in Waurika were sandbagged to help keep flood waters out.  In Cotton County, water was flowing over Highway 36 south of Route 70, over a road 1 to 2 miles south of Randlett, and over a roadway 3 miles south and 0.5 mile west of Devol during the evening hours of the 29th.  Near Comanche travel was reduced to one lane due to water covering Highway 81.  In Jefferson County, high water covered Highway 81 about 2 miles north of Addington.   Lightning strikes also caused damage during these storms.  A  home in Shattuck was struck by lightning.  The fire resulting from the lightning damaged electronic equipment and started a grass fire in the backyard of the home.  A fire from a lightning strike destroyed a trailer 2 miles west of Comanche.  A lightning strike to a home 6 miles north of Waurika resulted in minor damage.  In Quinton, lightning struck and killed several cattle.

A severe thunderstorm developed just ahead of a line of storm crossing from the mountains of Georgia into Oconee County, South Carolina.  This storm produced large hail for its entire journey across the upstate.  This hail caused an enormous amount of damage, especially to roofs and vehicles.  The hail piled up to great depths in some places such as Pickens where hail clogged storm drains and caused an urban flood which ruined much of a large store building under construction.  This storm also produced a well defined wall cloud over most of its path and a funnel was associated with the wall cloud as the storm moved south of Pickens, over Easley, and into Greenville.  It has been determined that the circulation reached the ground east of Easley along Highway 123.  There several cars were blown off the road while a "pipe shaped" funnel was directly overhead.  The condensation funnel and the main circulation never reached the ground apparently.  From all evidence the tornado could have been quite strong and long-lived had it fully developed.  The largest hail across the upstate was very close to the wall cloud structure.  The most wind damage was in West Greenville where a number of power lines were downed.  The funnel cloud was clearly visible there also but it has not been determined if the rotary wind caused the damage.  The funnel was followed by a number of law enforcement officers for quite a distance across Pickens and Greenville Counties.  A number of trees and power lines were blown down in parts of Spartanburg and Cherokee Counties from the same storm.  A second severe storm followed a few miles behind the first storm.  This storm also produced a great deal of large hail but no wind damage was reported with it.  Lightning set a home in North Spartanburg afire.

Strong to severe thunderstorms developed in a rapidly destabilizing airmass over northeast Georgia and upstate South Carolina.  This severe weather episode was confined to a very small area.  Three weak tornados were the first severe weather in the episode.  The first tornado developed as the parent thunderstorm grew into a significant storm.  This tornado spun a car around in the highway then lifted.  The same parent storm produced the longest lived tornado of the day.  The storm initially touched down at 1750 EST in the South Cove area of Lake Keowee north of Seneca where it tossed a large boat onto land and damaged several boathouses.  The tornado was clearly visible as a small but classic funnel on the ground and crossing the lake.  The tornado skipped along the ground intermittently for about 5 miles and was last spotted at the community of Keowee near Clemson.  Most damage was downed trees and power lines.  The third tornado in the Upstate came from a severe thunderstorm which also produced severe weather in Georgia.  This tornado was first viewed as a wall cloud and funnel by a trained spotter.  He was not initially able to determine that the storm completely reached the ground (view hindered by trees) but later information revealed that a mobile home was moved off its foundation, and trees were downed, in the specific area where he watched the storm dip down briefly.  The storm eventually developed a long-lived twin funnel configuration which was viewed by a number of people as it crossed the southern part of the city of Anderson.  Localized heavy rainfall caused several streams to overflow in Pickens County.  A number of roads and bridges were under water for a period of time.  The Olenoy River perhaps was the largest stream in flood.  Lightning struck a television transmitter site causing severe damage and knocking the station off the air for almost 6 hours.

A cluster of thunderstorms associated with an old meso-low pressure system left over from the previous day and early morning hours re-intensified as it moved rapidly from central Georgia into the southern part of the upstate. It began at Bradley in Greenwood County, crossed into Laurens County 10 miles north east of Greenwood at 1540 EST, and dissipated 5 miles south-southwest of Clinton.  The tornado was of F0 intensity with a width of 200 yards in Greenwood County.  Trees and power lines were blown down all along the path with fairly substantial damage in the Southern part of the city of Greenwood.  Chimneys were blown off some houses and large trees fell on some structures.  Not including hail damage, which will not be apparent until later, damage was estimated at $75,000 to $100,000.  In Laurens County the storm became a bit stronger reaching F1 intensity with a path width of 300 yards.  Most damage was around Cross Hill where a couple of mobile homes were damaged (one virtually destroyed), a steeple was blown off a church, and numerous trees were blown down.  Some trees fell on structures.  Damage, without hail considered, was in excess of $50,000.  The hailstorm associated with the supercell was very impressive.  Largest hail  was restricted to the  area very near the tornado with large amounts of marble to dime-size hail falling north of that area.  The tornado lifted before reaching Clinton but thunderstorm winds blew down some trees and power lines, blew shingles off roofs, and enormous amounts of golfball-size hail severely damaged cars and roofs.

Thunderstorms that developed over the northeast portion of Utah produced a high elevation tornado, large hail, and microburst winds. The tornado moved from southwest to northeast, touched down three times, and the path width was up to a half mile.  The tornado damaged around 1,000 acres of trees.  Most of the trees were uprooted, but some up to 18 inches in diameter were snapped.  Twenty acres was damaged in the first touchdown, around 600 acres in the second, and near 400 acres in the third.  The damage pattern of the trees in the area of the second touchdown confirmed the presence of a tornado.  Trees on the north side of the path were thrown south, and the ones on the south side were thrown north.  A troop of 125 scouts was camped near the area of the third touchdown.  No one was injured, but four vehicles were damaged by the uprooted trees.  This accounted for all of the damage.  The camp also experienced the 1.00-inch-diameter hail at this time.  The highest elevation the damage was found at was 10,800 feet.

An F2 tornado touched down in Polk County and traveled approximately 20 miles before it lifted.  Even though the tornado was not on the ground continuously, it still managed to cause extensive damage to several towns along its path.  The tornado initially touched down approximately 2.50 miles west of Cove, along Highway 4.  The storm passed through Cove where it damaged and destroyed several homes and businesses.  The tornado then struck the Hatfield area where it destroyed or damaged a number of homes.  The tornado continued moving northeastward and struck the southwest part of Mena.  In Mena, a large number of homes and businesses sustained damage.  Most of the buildings that were struck were either destroyed or received major damage.  Eleven people in Mena were treated for minor injuries.  A local park in Mena lost a number of large trees.  Some of these trees were over 100 years old.  A number of buildings in Mena were damaged as a result of trees falling on the structures.  The tornado finally lifted about three miles northeast of Mena, in the community of Hillcrest, where it destroyed a few mobile homes and damaged several others.  Initial estimates placed the damage at over $6 million.

Tornado touched down four miles south of Blue Hill in northern Webster county.  Two farm homes, and outbuildings were damaged.  Two 12,00 bushel grain bins were destroyed. A massive winter storm moved across central and southern Missouri producing snowfall up to 21 inches in isolated areas.  The heaviest snow extended along the extreme southern counties in Missouri up to Cape Girardeau where 9 to 21 inches fell.  Southwest City reported the most snow where thunderstorms helped to dump 21 inches, while Cape Girardeau and Springfield had 12 inches.  The airport at Cape Girardeau received 6 inches in an hour and 20 minutes. Snowfall was lighter to the north, but most of central Missouri had 5 to 10 inches.  St. Louis had just over 8 inches while Columbia reported 7. Travel was severely hampered, especially across southern Missouri where numerous accidents were reported.  Three known deaths all involved head-on collisions due to snow covered roads.  Local residents claim this was the strongest snow storm to hit the region in 14 years.

The tornado touched down with greater strength just before crossing into Ogemaw County where the Rifle River crosses the Ogemaw/Arenac County line.  The tornado then moved into Mills Township/Skidway Lake through a subdivision comprised mainly of mobile homes and cottages, reaching F2 strength.  It lifted briefly, about 0.75 mile northeast of the river, then touched down again and traveled another 6 miles, moving out of dense woods and into mostly open fields.  A total of 17 mobile  homes, 3 homes or cottages, 7 travel trailers, 4 garages, a barn, and 3 vehicles were destroyed or badly damaged.  Six people, in 3 of the mobile homes that were completely destroyed were warned by the approaching roar, and in each case, took some action that ultimately saved their lives.  Three were hospitalized with injuries.  The tornado lifted just west of Prescott.  Tree and power line damage occurred with the tornado itself, and up to 0.1 mile either side of the tornado path.  Structure damage and personal property loss in Ogemaw County is estimated at around $250,000, with another $110,000 in tree damage or loss.

Most of the individual cells were fairly short lived.  A few of the cells did produce severe weather.  These cells were the ones that were somewhat isolated, thus had less competition for available moisture.  One cell that became severe was over central Iowa. A tornado struck a subdivision five miles north of Albany and killed three people and injured another 27.  At least 42 homes were destroyed or severely damaged.  Also, fifteen mobile homes were completely destroyed by the F2 tornado.  The three fatalities occurred in a mobile home and all three victims bodies were blown 75 to 150 feet away from the dwelling.  Most of the damaged or destroyed homes were two story with brick or stucco exterior. Several residents noted that the tornado sounded like a freight train as it passed overhead.  One elderly lady stated that her dog became restless and started barking 20 minutes before the tornado struck her home.  Continuous lightning was observed by several residents prior to and after the tornado touchdown.   Several cars were destroyed by fallen trees or wind blown debris.  Most of the trees downed by the tornado winds were 60 to 70 feet tall Southern Pine.  Most trees were snapped in half and laid to rest in a general northeast direction. Property damage estimates topped $12 million dollars. The tornado stayed on the ground most of its lifetime and varied in width from one-quarter to one-half mile.  The damage path was approximately five miles long and ran in a SW to NE direction.  The forward speed of the tornado was 60 miles an hour. (F32M)(M14M)(M8M)

An intense late season storm moved out of the central Pacific toward southern Alaska on the morning of the 5th. By 1000 ADT the low was about 300 miles south of Kodiak Island with a central pressure of 975 mb. Ships in the southern quadrant of this low recorded sustained winds from 40 to 60 knots. Portions of Kodiak Island recorded peak wind gusts of 35 to 43 knots.

This low pushed a strong occluded front across the eastern Aleutians and Alaska Peninsula on the evening of the 25th, then into Bristol Bay early on the 26th. Strongest winds were reported from Cold Bay with a peak gust of 60 knots at 2233 and 2244 AST on the 25th. For a 3-hour period Cold Bay received sustained winds of 40 to 45 knots. Both Dutch Harbor and Port Heiden had 50 knot gusts. St. Paul recorded a peak gust of 39 knots at 2126 AST on the 25th. Thunderstorms dumped 2.00 to 5.00 inches of rain over southeast DuPage County and southern Cook County between 0900 CST and 1200 CST. Some of the heaviest rainfall amounts were 4.63 at Burr Ridge, 3.55 3.55 inches on the south side of Chicago and 3.08 at Burbank. According to the Illinois State Water Survey these rainfall amounts in a 2-hour period should have a recurrence interval of 30 to 60 years. As much as 6.00 to 6.50 inches fell in a 24-hour period from Burr Ridge to the south side of Chicago. This was one of the worst floods ever for south Chicago and the south suburbs. Interstate 90/94 (the Dan Ryan Expressway) and part of Interstate 57 were closed until 1800 CST due to flooding. Interstate 55 at route 83 was also closed for a short time. Many streets and viaducts were impassible. The Deep Tunnel flood control system under the south side of Chicago which holds 185 million gallons of water was filled. A warehouse roof collapsed in Blue Island due to the weight of rain water on it. 200 flights were canceled at O'hare International Airport and the were many delays at both O'hare and Midway. The heaviest rain was in southern Dupage County, southern Cook County and northern Lake County Indiana from Darien and Burr Ridge to Lake Calumet and Hammond.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Although river stages never really went below flood stage along the Mississippi River for an extended period of time, levels began to increase again dramatically toward the last half of the month. Flood levels were expected to reach near record levels toward the end of the month with hundreds of buildings damaged and most crops planted in flood plains underwater. Damage was primarily agricultural since most levees protecting the counties held through June. However, at Grafton, Illinois, near the confluence of the Illinois and Mississippi Rivers, numerous homes and businesses were flooded. The Mississippi River at Grafton had been above flood stage from March 25 through June 2. It dropped below flood stage for 4 days, before rising again on June 6. It stayed above flood through the rest of the month. Flooding continued into July.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As the low mentioned above continued to move northeast, the warm front pressed into Iowa and a dry line moved across the plains. Thunderstorms fired ahead of the dry line in northwest Iowa. The storms fired from a combination of the dry line and synoptic forcing. The first storms produced a 65 mph wind gust near Arnolds Park. The winds lifted boats from their moorings and overturned a couple of them. Several tornadoes were spawned by the storms. The strongest was in Lyon and Osceola Counties. The tornado was on the ground for about 10 miles. Though much of its path was over open country, the tornado did cause significant damage in Sibley. On its path, the tornado destroyed a cattle shed, blew out windows, and downed several trees. In Sibley, one roof was taken off of a house and a high school bus barn was taken down. Damage to the bus barn was around $150,000. There were several injuries in Sibley caused by flying glass and debris. Two other were injured as the collided while driving their cars in an attempt to outrun the tornado. Ironically, the call to action statement in the tornado warning for the area specifically advised NOT to try to outrun the tornado in your car. A second tornado was on the ground for about 7.5 miles. This tornado was not as strong, but did cause damage in Sioux County between Hospers and Sheldon. Several barns were taken down, along with a few silos. The tornado moved into the campus of the Northwest Iowa Community College, causing quite a bit of damage to the buildings. Other tornadoes touched down in the area in what turned out to be a small family of tornadoes. Damage was minor as the other tornadoes swept across open countryside. Lightning struck a house in Milford, starting a small fire.

Other tornadoes touched down in the area in what turned out to be a small family of tornadoes. Damage was minor as the other tornadoes swept across open countryside. Lightning struck a house in Milford, starting a small fire.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: June of 1993 was yet another cool and wet month...
High winds caused some damage in the Corydon area.
Another storm toppled several trees and power lines onto cars in the city of Clinton.
Excessive rains over Wayne and Appanoose Counties temporarily closed portions of Highway 2.
Monroe County reported road closures as well.
An example of the rain that fell during the evening of the 7th included 3.50 inches of rain in one hour at Promise City, in Wayne County.

Water was reportedly up to 3 feet deep on roads in Davis County at the peak of the flooding. Precipitation reports from Davis County indicated that 5.12 inches fell from the storms. Much of it, 3.00 to 4.00 inches, fell in less than 2 hours time.
High winds caused damage... at Bloomfield.
Heavy rainfall once again struck over Iowa causing significant river flooding. Widespread amounts in the 1.50- to 3.00-inch range fell over much of the lowa and Cedar River Basins.
Structural damage was also reported in Washington County in the Riverside area.
South of the city of Washington, high winds toppled a barn, killing 60 sows.
The storms touched off a brief tornado touch down in Boone County. During its brief life, one house was damage in the town of Fraser.
Another tornado touched down briefly at the Forest City Airport. A few buildings were damaged by this tornado.

The most significant hail occurred in Mitchell County. As was described by a local farmer there, large chunks of ice began to fall from the sky. The hail became larger and larger with some of the stones the size of softballs. Four farms in the county were badly damaged by the large hail.

A tornado was spawned by the storm southeast of the Osage area. Fortunately, it tracked across farm fields for the most part. It did strike four farmsteads, damaging one severely. Several small out buildings and barns were damaged but the farm houses were spared. On one farmstead, a pine tree was picked up and thrown over the house. A car was lifted and thrown 70 meters. Several calves and one pig were killed.
A trucker was injured on Highway 218 north of Ainsworth as high winds toppled his tractor-semitrailer.
South of this area, a small tornado touched down north of Wyman. It was on the ground for about 5 miles.
One house was damaged south of Columbus City. High winds threw a tree through the picture window of another house in Columbus City.
In Wapello, winds lifted a trailer and threw a child against a car. She was slightly injured.
Another cell became severe over Scott County. Tree damage and some power line damage occurred in Buffalo.

Urban flooding resulted from heavy rainfall in the city of Muscatine. Water was reportedly 2 feet deep for about an hour on some of the city streets. Several manhole covers were blown off from the water pressure.
Golfball-size hail fell in Buena Vista County at the onset of the storm development.
Three to six inches of rain fell in less than 2 hours in Buena Vista County, resulting in considerable flash flooding in the county.
Heavy rainfall in Cherokee County forced the closing of U.S. Highway 59 south of Cherokee for a period of time.
High winds in Onawa, in Monona County, physically moved a grain bin 75 feet from its moorings.

In what appeared to be a microburst, very strong winds blew through the Crushing area of Woodbury county. Tree branches were thrown through the window of one house. Relatives were sleeping over for the night and were on the floor. The wind pushed them across the room inside the house.
High winds blew down several trees in the northwest edge of Des Moines.
One tornado occurred in the southwest part of Iowa northeast of Red Oak. Little damage occurred as the tornado crossed open country, though it did take one trailer off of its foundation.
High winds in the Elliot area caused damage in east of Corning.

Flash Flooding occurred in Adams County from the heavy rainfall. In fact, 4.00 inches of rain fell on the town of Lenox in just one hours time. Runoff from the heavy rainfall caused rapid flooding with many bridges reported as under water for a time. In addition, there were reports of several bridges being washed out by the flash flooding.
High winds east of Mason City caused damage in the area, removing the roof from one building and destroyed one mobile home.
One of the stronger storms produced hail of 1.25 inch in diameter over the northern part of Warren County.
Two barns were destroyed north of Stanwood, in Cedar County, by microburst winds. Some large oak trees were blown down. Much of the damage was confined to a two city block size area.
South of May City, reports indicated that hail up to golfball-size had nearly completely covered the ground.
Later in the evening, lightning touched off a house fire in Milford.
Golfball-size hail fell in Clay County in the city of Webb.
High winds downed a grain silo in Palo Alto County near Ayrshire
High winds... caused damage west of Emmetsburg. A new flag pole was snapped off near Emmetsburg as well.
Significant structural damage was reported on one farmstead in Humboldt County at Bode. Minor structural damage was reported at several others around the area as well.
A tornado touched down briefly in Wright County south of the Clarion Airport. Witnesses reported seeing the tornado pick up dirt as it touched down in an open field.
Lightning struck a chimney in Ames. The force of the lightning bolt knocked bricks off of the chimney resulting in significant damage to five cars parked below.
A similar situation occurred in Fayette County in the Oelwein area. High winds ripped off the roof of a school there, causing in excess of $100,000 in damage.
In Winneshiek County, winds took off half of the junior high school roof in the town of Jackson Junction. Winds were reportedly near 85 mph. Damage to the roof was placed at $54,000.
In Allamakee County, trees and power lines were downed in the city of Waukon. Some barns were also damaged in the area.
High winds in Lansing caused roof damage to several homes in the city as winds estimated around 75 mph buffeted the city.
One thunderstorm moved through Linn County and produced high winds. The roof was blown off of a barn and a chicken house was blown off of its foundation near Palo.
Structural damage was reported in Mitchell County at Riceville as high winds swept through the town.
Several farms were damaged in Hardin County by high winds. On one of the farms several hogs were killed as a barn was destroyed near Hubbard.
One thunderstorm produced a funnel cloud in Chickasaw County for a brief period.
Another lightning strike occurred in Delaware County at Hopkinton. The lightning strike caused a small fire after striking a house there.
High winds leveled a house that was under construction north of Dyersville in Dubuque County.

The highest wind gust was a 78 mph wind gust recorded southeast of Conrad in Marshall County as one of the storms collapsed. Windows were blown out of houses there, the garage door was blown in on one house, and several light poles were toppled.
Lightning struck a house in the city of Waterloo. Minor damage occurred to the house with a small fire and damage to electrical appliances.
Other damage included... structural damage to houses in Jones County in Oxford Junction.

This rain event became the first really widespread event for the state. The rain fell over the state for an extended period of time; three days in fact... Flooding was moderate on the Iowa River above Coralville, the upper portion of the Cedar River, and the South Skunk River near Oskaloosa. General flooding, mostly minor, was recorded elsewhere around the state... Damage was difficult to estimate, but was well into the millions of dollars in terms of property losses. Crop damage was even more difficult to estimate...
Three-quarter inch diameter hail fell in Pella, for the only report of hail reaching severe criteria.
Another Cell collapsed in Butler County at Clarksville. It produced winds of 60 mph, downing several trees.
One cell collapsed east of Fairfield, resulting in high winds that downed many trees and some power lines.
Flash Flooding occurred in Marion County as 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain fell in a 45-minute time period. Highway 5 was under 6.00 to 7.00 inches of water for a period of time.

One barn was destroyed, however the hogs in the barn were able to escape. The tornado toppled over head stones in a cemetery southwest of Sigourney. The tornado briefly lifted as it crossed highway 149, then touched down and destroyed two out buildings and tore the side off an airplane hanger at the Sigourney Airport. Extensive damage was reported at the airport.

A more significant flash flood event took place over southern Benton and northern Iowa Counties. Reports indicated that up to 3.50 inches of rain fell in a 45-minute period of time there. Flooding occurred in many basements. Two county bridges were washed out in southern Benton County and one car was washed off the road southwest of Vinton... Three were killed in this incident, a 22-year-old female, a 19-year-old female who was 7 months pregnant, and the baby. (F19V, F22V, F0V)
The flooding was not as major in northern Iowa County. Flood waters abated within a few hours.

Another occurrence of downburst winds occurred in Benton County. There were numerous reports of damage around the county, mainly over the north half. Numerous trees downed and out buildings were damaged or destroyed.
Lightning struck the Law Enforcement building in Benton County. Computer equipment was damaged inside with damage in the $2,000 to $3,000 range.

A strong tornado touched down in Delaware County. The storm was tracked by weather radar as a mesocyclone. It touched down south and west of Manchester, causing major structural damage to a farm house. Later it picked up a car, spun it around, and turned it upside down north of Manchester. It moved into a forested area and finally lifted.

The third tornado was also quite strong. It touched down south of the Dubuque Airport. Tree branches fell out of the sky onto the runway at the Dubuque Airport. A large piece of sheet metal fell on top of the terminal building. A Northwest Airlink flight landed at the airport with tree branches attached to the aircraft. At least one farmstead was hit with a glancing blow. About $15,000 damage was reported with several propane tanks leaking following the damage caused by the tornado. The tornado tracked north-northeast across the extreme northwest tip of Illinois and into southwest Wisconsin where it finally dissipated.

The most significant high wind event took place in Clayton County, where a downburst wind caused significant damage. Four farm wagons were overturned, at least one power pole was snapped, and structural damage occurred on one farmstead.

Heavy rainfall over the upper Mississippi River Basin resulted in a large river crest as it came downstream through eastern Iowa. The levels crested just below the record crests of the great floods of 1965 and 1973... Major damage occurred along the river cities and farm land... The city of Davenport was very hard hit. Much of the downtown area was under water. Severe damage occurred there... Thousands and thousands of acres of farm land were under water. Crop losses were great. In addition, many farm levees were destroyed and overtopped by the high flood waters.

Hardest hit was eastern Emmet County. Between 1430 CST and 1800 CST, between 6.00 and 8.00 inches of rain fell around the Armstrong area... By 1620 CST, water was flooding over Highway 9. An hour later, water was over two places on Highway 9, Highway 15 along the Emmet-Kossuth County line was overtopped with water, and numerous gravel roads were closed due to flash flooding.

Northern Kossuth County was affected by the flash flooding, though not to the extent that Emmet County was. Two to three inches of rain fell in a short period of time, under 2 hours, causing flash flooding.

Rainfall occurred over the northwestern part of Iowa. In the upper half of the Little Sioux River Basin, 1.50 inches of rain was reported with 1.50 to 3.00 inches falling over the south half. Flooding was minor and generally restricted to the lower part of the Little Sioux River. Much of the flooding was caused by levees and levee failure.
Lightning also struck one house in New London, setting it on fire.
The only other lightning strike reported was south of the Mt. Pleasant Airport, where lightning took down a utility pole.
One storm did produce high winds in Des Moines County at Mediapolis. About $46,000 damage was done on one farmstead when winds downed a machine building.

The most significant rainfall report came from Henry County, where a report of 6.50 inches of rainfall in 15 minutes was received from New London. Other reports from the area included 3.00 inches in Burlington, 5.00 inches in Fort Madison, and a total rainfall in New London of 10.10 inches. Many areas reported 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rainfall in under 2 hours. Flooding was widespread in Henry County due to the heavy rainfall. Numerous roads were closed and under water, with the water covering several bridges. The sheriff reported the Skunk River was out of its banks and had risen 30 inches in the 3-hour period between 1630 CST and 1930 CST. Roads and bridges along the river were going under water at that time. The town of New London reported extensive flooding with many roads blocked off.
In Des Moines County, U.S. Highway 61 had water 3 feet deep covering it in some areas south of Burlington.
In Jones County for example, heavy rainfall resulted in water running over roads in the Wyoming area at a depth of 3 feet.
Route 136 was reportedly under up to 8.00 inches of water for a 5- to 10-mile stretch.
Flash Flooding in Van Buren County was heaviest over the southeast part of the county, where many roads were overtopped with water.

General rainfall occurred over the eastern part of Iowa on the 24th and early on the 25th. Rainfall amounts were in the 1.00 to 2.00 inch range in an area from near Dubuque down toward Coralville Reservoir to Keosaqua and all areas eastward. Rainfall was generally around 3.00 inches or more along the Mississippi River. As has been the case with most of the rainfall events this month, a significant flash flooding event preceded the general flooding event. As the water from the flash floods, as mentioned above most of these, flowed into the rivers a period of general flooding followed. Moderate river flooding occurred on the lower portions of the Iowa River, especially at Wapello, and the Cedar River, especially at Conesville.
Lightning struck a power pole there, knocking out power and telephone service in the city of Greely.
Baseball-size hail covered the ground 6 miles north of Harlan.

One cell dropped hail in a swath about 2 miles wide and nearly 20 miles long. In the center of this band, the hail was anywhere from golfball to softball size... Crop damage was severe. Reports of 75 percent crop destruction were common within the hail swath.

Northwest of Little Sioux, hail up to the size of golfballs completely covered the ground. There was enough hail on the ground to for drifts of hail to form. Needless to say, crop damage in the area was significant.
A barn was damaged northwest of Massillon by the high winds. The barn was damaged and several head of cattle were killed. Trees were also uprooted in the area.

Rainfall reports of 4.00 to 6.00 inches were received around the Coralville Dam area. The Dam site officially recorded 3.60 inches of rain. There was an unofficial report of 6.00 inches just south of Iowa City. The heavy rains caused a two-fold problem. First, the ground in the area was already saturated. This caused considerable run off and closed several roads. The second problem was with the Coralville Reservoir itself. The reservoir was near capacity and the heavy rainfall nearly caused it to overflow.
High winds did cause some damage in the Buffalo area of Scott County.
There was a report of wind damage in Mills County with a few trees being downed.
Hail a little smaller than golfball size pelted the Andover area of Clinton County.

General rainfall over the 4-county area was in the 1.50- to 2.50-inch range... Reports indicated that some of the rivers in the area rose over a foot in less than 5 minutes as the runoff entered the river system. Agricultural areas reported widespread flooding.
The heaviest rainfall reported was in the Silver City area of Mills County, where 5.00 inches of rain was reported by an unofficial observer there.
Considerable street flooding was reported in Clarinda for example.

A storm collapsed in Page County over the city of Clarinda. The microburst winds caused significant damage in the city. A new bowling alley and an A & W root beer stand were damaged. A dealership in town had a significant part of its roof removed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several tornadoes were spawned during the evening. Most of them were brief touch downs and caused little damage. Such was the case in Greene County, where two brief touch downs occurred in open countryside. An earlier touch down north of Sibley, in Ocseola County, did little more than cause tree damage. Two tornadoes touched down in Pocahontas County. The first was a brief touch down. The second was on the ground between Havelock and Gilmore City. Much of the area it traversed was open country. A few farmsteads were affected with most damage to out buildings. One farmstead received significant damage northwest of Gilmore City just before the tornado lifted. The storm was still strong as it moved across the city. Damage was substantial at a lumber yard as high winds lifted the roof from the building and threw it into a house across the street. The lumber yard building was virtually destroyed it. The longest tornado track cut across three counties. The tornado touched down in Boone County and cut a path across southern Story County into northeast Polk County. This tornado had a very intermittent track and lifted several times or remained just above ground. As it moved across northeast Polk County, the storm weakened. Damage was limited due to its intermittent track and the fact that that part of the state is not heavily populated. The storm moved into Jasper County, but by then was below severe levels and just produced heavy rainfall and some small hail. During the late night hours, two tornadoes touched down in Scott County. One north of New Liberty was only a brief touch down and caused no significant damage. The second was north of the Stockton area. A couple was camping in Scott County north of Stockton. The tornado rolled their mobile home. The husband received several cuts and bruises. His wife sustained a broken arm and cuts that required 24 stitches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An earlier touch down north of Sibley, in Ocseola County, did little more than cause tree damage.
Rainfall was intense in Dickinson and Emmet Counties. During a period of 3 to 4 hours, 6.00 to 7.00 inches of rain fell into an area that was already flooded. Flash Flooding was widespread.
To give some idea of rainfall rates, Ocheyedan received 3 inches in 45 minutes, Allendorf picked up 2.80 inches in just 30 minutes.
Rainfall was intense in Dickinson and Emmet Counties. During a period of 3 to 4 hours, 6.00 to 7.00 inches of rain fell into an area that was already flooded. Flash Flooding was widespread.
A barn was also burn in Emmet County in Independence Township after lightning struck the barn.

The largest hail fell in Emmet County in the Ringsted area. Hail as large as 3.50 inches in diameter pelted the area with many windows reportedly broken out. Reports indicate that north of the Estherville area, baseball-size hail covered the ground.
Lightning struck a mobile home in Cero Gordo County at Rockwell. It was set on fire, completely destroying it.
In Palo Alto County at Ruthven... lightning struck a house. The chimney was knocked off of the house and one wall of the house was bowed after the incident.
In Palo Alto County at Ruthven, grain bins were destroyed by high winds...

The tornado rolled their mobile home. The husband received several cuts and bruises. His wife sustained a broken arm and cuts that required 24 stitches.

An apparent downburst swept the Stockton area with winds between 90 and 100 mph.

In what turned out to be the most widespread significant rainfall event of the month took shape during the afternoon and evening hours of the 29th. Heavy rainfall was widespread... Widespread rainfall of 1.50 to 2.00 inches fell over the entire Mississippi watershed in Iowa. These amounts were also common over the Grand (also known as the Thompson) River Basin. Local amounts in this area were in the 3 inch or greater range. The heavy rainfall caused significant rises of more than 2 feet on many rivers.
As it passed over the city of Glenwood, in Mills County, it dropped golfball-size hail on the town.

Rainfall of 2.00 to 6.00 inches fell in Union and Cass Counties. As has been the case for much of the Spring and early Summer, ground conditions were very saturated. The rain ran off quickly causing flash flooding across the county.
As the thunderstorms moved across Appanoose County, lightning struck a Pastors house in Unionville. Damage was minor, however a small fire was started. That did result in some damage.
Wheat crops sustained $100,000 in damage to 1500 acres.
Hail up to golfball-size caused about $400,000 damage to 3,000 acres of wheat, corn and milo.
Hail up to golfball-size damaged 2,000 to 3,000 acres of crops with about $400,000 damage.
Tornado lasted 5 minutes moving to the southeast at over 20 mph over open country.
A brief tornado was moving southeast over open country.
Two grain silos were blown down and damage occurred to roofs in the area.
Winds to 78 knots were observed on wind equipment.
Two mobile homes were damaged by winds.
Trees measuring 6 inches in diameter were knocked down.
Large tree limbs were broken off by Thunderstorm wind.
Total crop damage was reported in a 5- to 6-mile-wide path from 5 miles south of Syracuse to 11 miles south of Kendall.
A wheat field was destroyed by hail just south of Elk City, causing about $125,000 damage.
Baseball-size hail broke car windows in Dearing.

In the Indian Hills area just north of Coffeyville, 3.00-inch hail fell for almost 20 minutes punching holes in garage roofs. Damage in the Coffeyville area included broken windows and roof damage on residences as well as extensive vehicle damage.
Winds to 50 mph accompanied the hail.
Winds to 50 mph accompanied the hail.

A Fort Riley soldier was killed when a tree fell on his car during a severe thunderstorm that brought widespread damage to the base and nearby areas. The death occurred on 8th Street in the Camp Forsysth area. The tree was uprooted and pinned the man in his car. He was pronounced dead about 1 hour later at a local hospital. The severe storm caused numerous power outages and dropped very heavy rain in a short time. (M34V)
Strong winds blew down signs on the Kansas Turnpike.

In Sumner County 20 square miles, or about 10,000 acres, of wheat were damaged by a hail storm... The storm also spawned a brief tornado that touched down in a park on the southeast side of Wellington, but there was no danage.
Hail fell at the Marshall Air Field on the military reservation.
High winds estimated to 60 or 70 mph accompanied the hail and downed several trees and limbs.
In Sumner County 20 square miles, or about 10,000 acres, of wheat were damaged by a hail storm.
Hail up to 1.00 inch in diameter accompanied the high winds.
A hailstorm dropped 0.75-inch hail to a depth of 3 inches.
High winds uprooted trees in the Lake Shawnee area along with marble-size hail.
High winds downed trees and caused power outages. Marble-size hail was also common.
Strong Thunderstorm wind blew over an apple tree near Dalton.
Winds estimated to over 60 mph uprooted trees, downed power lines and blew out windows at a farmstead.
High winds over 60 mph blew a patrol car off the road and caused tree damage.
Large hail caused damage to cars, roofs and crops in the area.
Storm watchers reported a brief tornado hit in an open field. A well defined rotating wall cloud and several funnels were also visible as the storm moved southeast.
Hail about the size of baseballs fell in the area.
Several funnel clouds were sighted in and around the Westmoreland area moving southeast.
Very heavy rainfall also caused flooding of low lying and poor drainage areas. Several motorists along U.S. Highway 24 reported zero visibility and had to pull over.
High winds broke out windows and tore off roofs. Very heavy rain fell across the area causing temporary flooding of low lying and poor drainage areas.
This tornado touched down over open country and remained over open country until it dissipated.
This tornado touched down over open country, blew the siding off of a steel shed at one farmstead, and dissipated shortly thereafter.
This tornado touched down over open country, then destroyed the roof of a barn before dissipating.
Winds blew a truck into a ditch. Large trees were also knocked down in this area.
Golfball-size hail, driven by Thunderstorm wind, damaged wheat and broke windows along a 4-mile path. Trees were also blown down.
Heavy rain caused roads in the Syracuse area to flood. As much as 1 foot of water covered some roads for a short period of time.
Hail damaged 5,000 acres of wheat that resulted in a $750,000 loss.
Large trees were knocked down and semi-trailers were also blown over.

A lone thunderstorm developed in front of a line of thunderstorms. A tornado was reported by the public in open farmland. This tornado touched down briefly. The thunderstorm that produced this tornado continued to move to the east.

The thunderstorm that produced the tornado in Pawnee County continued to move to the east and was followed by a line of severe thunderstorms. Downburst winds did extensive damage in the Burdett and Rozel areas... Every telephone pole in a 3.5-mile stretch from 1 mile northwest of Rozel to 3 miles southwest of Rozel was knocked down. Two large metal plated grain bins were dented by the winds... A welded guard rail on a bridge was snapped off and carried 25 yards over the bridge.
Winds blew off a roof to a garage and damaged other roofs in the area.
Telephone poles were knocked down between Ness City and Bazine.
Large trees and tree limbs were knocked down.
Large tree limbs were knocked down by Thunderstorm wind.
Trees and telephone poles were knocked down in the Hanston area.
Telephone poles were knocked down.
Heavy rain caused some roads in Dodge City to be flooded.

This event began on the 19th and continued through the end of June and into July. A persistent heavy rain producing weather pattern that had anchored itself over much of Northcentral and Central Kansas had finally begun to take its toll... Damage caused by erosion and gullying affected 3,000 acres... Ten miles of fence was damaged or destroyed. Eight farm dwellings and buildings and damage totaling $80,000.
Tornado moved 10 mph east-southeast over open country.
Strong Thunderstorm wind blew over trees in Durham.
Tree limbs were blown down at 21st Street and Hillside.
Power lines were blown down at 2nd and Hillside Streets.
Cars were blown off the road by Thunderstorm wind at 61st Street and Interstate 135.

Heavy rainfall caused flooding of numerous intersections and underpasses in and around the city of Lawrence. Power was knocked out by lightning, falling lines or water in transformers. Some roads were temporarily closed due to high water.
Wind gusts of over 70 knots were measured at the emergency operations center just before power was lost.
Two large trees were uprooted near downtown in Winfield. The high winds also ripped shingles from roofs and knocked down power lines.
A brief tornado was reported over open country.
Hail and high winds caused $2 million crop losses and property damage near $150,000.
A tornado moved south at 40 mph.
A brief tornado was reported over open country.
Large branches were blown down.
There were reports of tree damage in a few sections of town.

Many roofs to homes and mobile homes were damaged or destroyed on the east side of Garden City. Two mobile homes were knocked off their foundations. A semi trailer truck was knocked over. Six hanger doors at the Garden City Airport were blown off. One hangar door was blown into a Aerostar airplane parked inside the hangar. A modular classroom at Victor Ornlelas Elementary School was knocked off its foundation.
Large trees were knocked down in the Minneola area. A camping trailer was blown over. Windows to some houses in Minneola were also blown out.
Large trees were knocked down by Thunderstorm wind.
Winds gusting to 72 mph were measured at Kansas-Nebraska Power.
Street signs were blown down in and around the Protection area.
A farmer lost 16 head of cattle when the tree they were resting under was struck by lightning. Ten cows and 6 calves were killed, for a total loss of $15,000.
Large limbs were blown from trees.

Two outbuildings were blown down and two mobile homes were tipped over in Galena.
Strong Thunderstorm wind knocked large tree limbs onto cars and houses and uprooted trees. The winds also took part of the roof off the American Legion shelter at the town park.

Three to five inches of rain fell across Allen County and flooded State Street in Iola. The heavy rain also caused low-lying areas across the county to become flooded and some secondary roads had to be closed.
Three to five inches of rain caused the closure of Highway 160 south of McCune. Gravel roads were washed out across the county due to the heavy rain.
Up to 4.00 inches of rain fell in northeast Labette County, causing a small stream to exceed its banks and flood a county road. Other creeks in the northeast part of the county were also flooded.
Three to five inches of rain forced the closure of Highway 7 between Scammon and Columbus.
Large trees blown down by Thunderstorm wind.
There were reports of tree damage in a few sections of town.

Large tree limbs knocked down.

High winds knocked down trees and power lines and caused widespread damage in the city.

Hail about the size of a baseball pelted the area.
A weak, short-lived tornado touched down on the Fort Riley firing range area causing no damage.
A tornado hit briefly in an open field causing no damage.

A tornado destroyed two farmsteads and damaged several others along with several adjacent outbuildings, sheds and machinery... A man rode out the tornado in the cab of a pickup truck that was parked in shed that was demolished by the tornado.
High winds associated with a slow moving supercell thunderstorm caused widespread damage to much of Manhattan. Trees were uprooted, power lines torn down and roofs and buildings damaged...

The same supercell thunderstorm that produced a tornado near Keats dropped another weak tornado in the Hunters Island area south of Manhattan. Substantial damage occurred to about six or eight homes and buildings.
Another weak tornado dropped from the slow moving supercell and hit along Deep Creek east of Highway K177. Only minor damage was noted.
Winds estimated to at least 70 mph tore down power lines, trees and caused some damage to buildings. The wind was accompanied by torrential rainfall that produced widespread flooding.
High winds knocked down trees in and around the city.
A weak tornado briefly hit in an open field.

Torrential rainfall of 3.00 to 5.00 inches in about 2 hours caused widespread flash flooding in and around the city of Manhattan. Many streets were closed due to high water, sometimes 2 to 3 feet deep.
Winds estimated at 70 mph hit the east side of Tuttle Creek Lake.

Torrential rainfall of 3 to 5 inches in 2 to 3 hours caused widespread flooding in Wamego and the southern quarter of the county. Basements were flooded along with most streets and roads. U.S. Highway 24 was closed due to high water. Several businesses were damaged when flood waters overspread the area.
Several funnel clouds were sighted northwest of Rossville and dissipated as they moved east.
Very heavy rainfall caused flash flooding generally between Blue Rapids and Frankfort. Some roads especially in rural areas were flooded or washed out.
Heavy rains caused flash flooding across the southwestern part of the county.
Strong winds destroyed several barns and downed trees and power lines.
Trees and power lines were blown down.
Reported in the northeastern portion of the county.
Large hail pierced house roofs and dented cars. Also several large greenhouses were badly damaged.
Hail which fell east of Cropper destroyed several fields of tobacco.
Hail was reported in both Worthville and Owenton.
Large trees were blown down about 3 miles west of Owenton.
Golfball-size hail damaged several vehicles west of Versailles.
Several homes and mobile homes sustained damage as trees fell on their roofs. Vehicles were also damaged by falling tree limbs. Trees and power lines were blown down throughout the county.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down from Oscar to Bandana and to Ingleside. It removed roofs from many homes and or partially destroyed roofs of homes and businesses.

Thunderstorms in bow echo pattern created a damage path from 10 to 20 miles wind on both sides of the Ohio River. Structural damage to roofs and homes through populated areas from Kevil, Ragland, and Woodville, Heath and west Paducah and the city of Paducah. Many trees and power lines down with power outages up to 2 2 days at some locations. Injuries were minor.
Strong winds downed trees and power lines. Many homes were damaged by the falling trees. There were several minor injuries.
A small tornado was reported at Oak Level (16 miles southeast of Paducah). Structural damage to homes and some small businesses was reported. Numerous trees and power lines were also blown down.
Strong wind overturned mobile homes and damaged roofs on buildings throughout the county. Numerous trees and power lines were blown down. Several minor injuries were reported.
Wind damage to many homes throughout the county. Most damage was to roofs. Many trees and power lines were blown down.
Strong winds downed trees and left over 2,000 customers without electricity around Cadiz.
Wind damaged homes and, numerous trees and power lines were blown down.
Wind damaged roofs of homes from Princeton north to the Critendon County Line.
A derecho resulted in numerous trees broken and uprooted along with several roofs damaged or destroyed.
Heavy rains falling in a short period of time forced creeks and streams out of their banks. Several roads and low areas were flooded.

A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the county. Providence, Dixon, and Sebree were hard hit. Throughout the county, 15 homes and 30 barns were destroyed. Tree and debris clean-up alone amounted to $45,000 in Dixon and $13,000 in Providence.
A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the county. The northern part of the county was hit hardest with 6 homes and 14 barns being destroyed. In addition, 87 homes sustained roof damage.
A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the southern part of the county. Numerous trees, tobacco plants, and road signs were blown down.
A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the northern part of the county. Numerous trees, tobacco and corn plants, and road signs were blown down.

A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the county. The hardest hit community was Beech Grove where every road was impassable due to downed trees. One person was injured when his home was destroyed with him in it. Five mobile homes were destroyed across the county. Twenty percent of the tobacco barns were completely destroyed with the loss estimated at over $1 million according to the county agricultural agent.

A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the county. The hardest hit area was the northern half of the county. Numerous homes and mobile homes sustained damage. Roads were impassable due to downed trees and signs.
A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the southern part of the county. Numerous trees and road signs were blown down.

A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the county. Centertown in the western part of the county was hardest hit although trees were blown down throughout the county. Many homes sustained damage to roofs and siding.
Hail caused extensive crop damage throughout the southern end of the county.
A person was injured by lightning in Independence.
Numerous trees were blown down and windows were blown out of a house in Salyersville.

A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the county. At least 30 homes and mobile homes sustained major damage with another 30 reporting minor damage. Hard hit was Morgantown where schools were also damaged. Two children were slightly injured when the mobile home they were in was blown over. The Civil Defense Director estimated 75 to 95 percent of the roads in Butler County were blocked due to downed trees.
Trees and power lines were blown down.
Hail reported in Paintsville.
Trees and power lines were blown down throughout the county.
A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the southern part of the county. Trees and road signs were blown down and there was minor damage to some homes in the Pellville area.
A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the county. Homes were damaged in Caneyville and trees were uprooted throughout the county.
Trees were blown down 3 miles north of Prestonsburg.
Downburst in Visalia pushed a mobile home 20 feet down a hill. A large section of a nearby roof was blown off. A small garage was also destroyed. Winds were estimated between 80 and 90 mph.
Hail reported at Dewey Lake State Park.
Trees and power lines were blown down throughout the county.
A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the county. Homes were damaged around Sweeden and Lindseyville. Trees were uprooted throughout the county.
A derecho resulted in widespread damage across the county. Trees were blown down throughout the county.
Power lines were blown down in Falmouth.
A derecho resulted in trees blown down throughout the county.
Barns and outbuildings were destroyed. Trees and power lines were blown down.
Trees and power lines were blown down.
A derecho resulted in trees and power lines blown down throughout the county.
Numerous trees were blown down throughout the northern two thirds of the county.
Trees and power lines were blown down in Falmouth.

High winds destroyed a boat dock near Holmes Bend. Downed trees in the area also damaged homes, causing millions of dollars in damages.
A derecho resulted in trees and power lines blown down throughout the county.

A derecho resulted in trees blown down throughout the county.
A tornado briefly touched down about 1 mile south of Visalia. Large trees were uprooted and some small outbuildings were damaged.
Strong winds pushed a car several feet in a parking lot in Critenden.
Trees were blown down in Union.

Trees and power lines were blown down in the eastern portion of the county.
Strong winds damaged homes and buildings. Trees and power lines were also blown down. Some of the worst damage occurred around New Haven.

Many homes and barns were damaged as strong winds blew across the area. Most of the county was without electricity as many power lines were blown down. Some of the worst damage occurred around Burgin.
Trees and power lines were blown down in and around Campbellsville.
Trees and power lines were blown down.
High winds damaged homes and buildings across the county. Many trees and power lines were also blown down. Some of the worst damage occurred around Buffalo.
Strong winds damaged homes and buildings in and around Springfield.
The county rescue squad reported flooding in many parts of the county.

A storm with winds of 75 to 100 mph, knocked down power lines, barns, silos and hundreds of trees. Some homes were extensively damaged by falling trees. Destruction was reported the worst in Lebanon, Holy Cross, and Loretio.
Winds in excess of 70 mph damaged homes and buildings across the county. Hundreds of trees were blown down. One lady sustained a fracture to her ankle as a result of the storm.
Trees and power lines were blown down.
Winds in excess of 65 mph damaged homes and buildings throughout the county. Over 300 people reported at least some damage to homes. Many trees and power lines were also blown down.
Strong winds damaged homes and destroyed barns and outbuildings. Many trees and power lines were also blown down.
Winds downed trees and power lines throughout the county. Some of the worst damage occurred around Berea. Several homes were damaged and one person suffered a broken arm.
A radio station reported extensive damage occurred in the Meta area.
Winds estimated between 60 and 80 mph downed trees, flattened barns and knocked part of a two story brick wall at Stanford Elementary through the first floor library roof.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down across the county. Several automobiles and 33 homes or buildings were damaged as well. Most of the damage occurred in Broadhead.
Trees and power lines were blown down throughout the county.
Strong winds damaged several mobile homes and barns. Trees and power lines were also blown down.
Trees and power lines were blown down in London.
Beattyville police reported the roof blown off the St. Helens school in Beattyville. Also at least 75 trees were blown down.
Trees and power lines were blown down across the county. A mobile home was blown off its foundation in the small community of Pace Creek.
Strong winds damaged some homes and buildings around the county. Also many trees and power lines were blown down.
Many trees were blown down throughout the county and numerous outbuildings were destroyed.
Trees and power lines were blown down throughout the county.

Roofs were blown off several homes in the Big Branch area. Many roads were blocked by downed trees.

The tornado damaged a house, garage and trees on the north side of Interstate 44 before crossing the interstate and damaging a truck driving school. The 3-mile-long and 50-yard-wide damage path was not continuous, and the tornado produced F0 to occasional F1 damage.

Eight-hour rainfall totals included 2.75 inches at Penn Hills, 2.27 inches at Amnity, 2.30 inches at Kingston, 2.15 inches at New Lexington, and 1.92 inches at Berlin. Lightning struck a house creating a large hole in the roof. The home owner was injured as current flowed through the electrical wiring of the house and into his arm. He was turning on the light switch at the time.
Wires and trees down at Summerville. Shingles were blown off the roof of a house.
Lightning struck a drug store in Punxsutawney dislodging bricks that fell onto parked cars.
Two women were injured by lightning while standing in a parking lot in Jefferson Township. The lightning struck a nearby tree. The women were knocked to the ground.
Winds of 70 mph with large flying debris was reported by a Skywarn observer.
A water treatment plant was struck by lightning at Nanty Glo damaging two water pumps.
In Ebensburg, the EOC radio tower was damaged by lightning.

The combination of straight line wind and a weak tornado was responsible for damage to several communities in Cambria County. From Spinaly City to Coupon (approximately 3 miles), there was a 1-mile-wide area of wind damage. Structural damage occurred to several homes along with widespread tree damage.

A distinct path of damage was noted from the St. Josephs Cemetery to just east of the community of Coupon. One resident said he saw trees flying through the air, with one tree flying right over the top of his house. A total of twenty residences were damaged. One swimming pool and a small shed were completely destroyed.

A severe hailstorm deposited several inches of hail in southwest Westmoreland County. Between $10,000 and $15,000 in damage was done to the Martins, Flower and Shrub Greenhouses in Rostraver Township. Four greenhouse coverings were destroyed along with numerous plants. Apples were knocked off trees and many gardens were stripped of foliage. The hail which covered the ground took 2.5 hours to melt. Largest hailstones were around 1.50 inches in diameter.

Numerous trees were downed across the county downing powerlines and blocking roads. In Huntingdon, 1.00-inch hail was reported, and a locust tree fell onto a house. There were also reports of street and poor drainage flooding.

Numerous trees were downed across the county downing powerlines and blocking roads. In Huntingdon, 1.00-inch hail was reported, and a locust tree fell onto a house. There were also reports of street and poor drainage flooding.
Three-quarter-inch hail and trees were downed at Mount Pleasant. Some minor roof damage also occurred.
Three-quarter-inch hail and trees were downed at Mount Pleasant. Some minor roof damage also occurred.
Five children were injured when lightning struck the ground near them at the Maxwell Elementary School in Hempfield Township.

From Everson to Wooddale, a tornado destroyed 3 mobile homes and two barns. One of the mobile homes overturned and injured a 45-year-old women. The second mobile home the roof tore off, which landed into a nearby fire station causing $20,000 in damage to the Bullskin Township fire station. A firemen at the station was injured by flying debris. Siding was torn from several other homes, and a porch roof was ripped from a house. A total of 23 homes, 9 mobile homes, 3 barns, a private school, and 1 business received minor damage. Along Route 1047, east of Scottdale, a 1,000 pound horse was seen flying through the air before landing in a nearby creek. The horse underwent surgery for an 8-inch gash to the chest. Five other horses were also fifted off the ground, and carried several hundred yards.
In addition to the 1.00-inch hail report, trees were reported down and there was some urban flooding.

Strong downburst winds caused significant damage to a farm in Shippensburg. The damage included peeling back a metal roof on a hay barn, blowing a 2.25-ton forage wagon on its side, 6 feet from its wheel impression, destroying two hay wagons after blowing them 200 yards, breaking a dozen windows and blowing down a chimney. The winds also split trees vertically and knocked down a utility pole. A fiberglass hutch was blown away with a calf in tow. In other parts of the town, trees were uprooted and power was knocked out. Golfball-size hail also accompanied the storm. Several funnel clouds were spotted with this storm and it is possible that some of the damage may have been caused by an F0 tornado. An investigation of the event; however, indicated that straight line winds were the primary cause of the damage.
One-inch hail fell and numerous trees were downed.
One-inch hail fell and numerous trees were downed.
Large hail broke numerous windows, dented aluminum siding and cars, cracked windshields and destroyed flowerbeds. Numerous wires were taken down by the wind, resulting in several power outages.
Wind knocked down powerlines, disrupting power to western areas of the county.
Trees and wires downed with power outages resulting.
Numerous reports of golfball-size hail across the northern part of Lawrence County.
Fifty trees downed by Thunderstorm wind, one tree landed on a mobile home.
Large trees down by Thunderstorm winds.
In Potter Township along Route 18, a tree fell onto a house.

A New Sewickley Township Patrolman was struck by lightning while filling his cruiser with gas. The 41-year-old police officer said the shock came through the gas nozzle knocking him to the ground. The shock numbed his hand and made his head throb. He said, 'its like I have a thousand needles in me.'

Twenty-four hour rainfall totals in western Pennsylvania reached nearly 3.00 inches in some locals. In Lawrence County, heavy rain caused a section of roof and front wall of a building to collapse at New Castle. Croton Avenue was closed for several hours from the debris. In Mercer County, at Greenville, heavy rain caused the roof of the Advantage Auto Parts Store to collapse. Damage was estimated at $45,000. An observer in Greenville reported 1.25 inches of rain, falling in less than 20 minutes.

Numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines in Hickory, Neshannock, Pulaski, Scott and Shenango, townships. A mobile home was knocked off its foundation at Harlansburg. Another mobile home was split in half by a giant oak tree in New Castle. Several houses were damaged by fallen trees and two cars were crushed by downed trees. Numerous county roads were closed from fallen trees and flooding. Covert Road in Union and North Beaver Townships was closed from flooding, and State Route 351 near Enon Valley was flooded by four feet of water. In Neshannock Township, a creek near Pulaski Road expanded to about 75-feet wide, breaking off a 50-foot section of land surrounding a mobile home. The water uprooted several large trees.

Lightning struck a radio antenna across the street and jumped to a Penn DOT employee standing in an open doorway of the maintenance building. The 40-year-old man was treated and released from the area hospital.
Trees were down and also laying on wires.

Funnel clouds were sighted at Salladasburg and Jersey Shore between 1123 EST and 1125 EST, but a ground survey could not confirm the reports. A ground survey in Trout Run showed that this damage was consistent with downburst winds of 60 to 70 knots. The downburst hit a mobile home broadside and rolled it over onto its roof. Two people were in the structure at the time, but only one person received minor injuries. Several other mobile homes in the park received minor damage. Within 0.25 mile of the mobile home park, an old barn was blown down and three others damaged. Numerous trees were downed in an area that was no more than 200 yards wide and 0.25 mile long. A few houses and hunting cabins were damaged when trees fell on them. All trees, the mobile home and the barn were blown down toward the north. In Williamsport, trees were uprooted. About 1,000 customers lost power throughout the county.
Numerous trees were down near Bentley Creek, Canton and Monroeton from 1145 EST to 1200 EST. Also, funnel clouds were spotted at Athens and Ulster between 1130 EST and 1135 EST.
Spotters reported large trees blown down.
