Lightning struck St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church. The Steeple caught on fire and was so badly damaged that 20 feet of it had to be removed from the church.
Carbon county emergency management reported trees and many large limbs down.

Emergency management and PennDot reported many large limbs down, some power lines down, and several trees uprooted throughout the county. Most damage was in the east section of the county southeast of Allentown. A wind gust of 58 mph was recorded at Allentown Airport.

Police from Easton and the dispatcher from the Northampton county EMA called with reports of trees uprooted as well as many large limbs and wires down throughout the city of Easton and in Wilson borough. Power outages affected 8,300 residents.
Large trees were downed at Somerset.

This small and short-lived tornado was first spotted near North Brandywine JHS and travelled southeast crossing route 30. The tornado veered southwest after crossing route 340 and dissipated in an area east of the Veterans Administration Medical Center. A funnel cloud was spotted aloft during a large portion of the route. The hardest hit area was apparently near Caln. Crews worked through the night to clear dozens of trees and branches, tangled wires, replace fallen utility poles and repair damaged transformers. The hospital was forced to us emergency generator power. Just down the road from the hospital, a barn built in 1812 was turned to rubble. The tornado pushed the silo about 6 inches off its base and collapsed the roof, crushing farm equipment inside. Newly planted crops were blown in all directions and there were 7,000 power outages throughout the county. An AT&T employee was killed when a falling tree struck his vehicle as he was driving north on North Caln Road about 1530 EST. The tree also snapped two electric wires on the way down, preventing rescue workers from getting to the man. (M45V)
Trees were downed and small hail was reported.
Dime-size hail was reported by a weather spotter.

Trees were uprooted, broken and twisted off in all directions. The damage was on top of a hill. An eye witness saw the tornado tear up the trees after heavy rain and half dollar-size hail had moved through the area.

An eye witness saw the tornado tear up the trees after heavy rain and half dollar-size hail had moved through the area. At 1715 EST trees were downed 4W of Hop Bottom. An investigation by NWS personnel indicated that it may have been an F0 tornado, but there was no definite confirmation of existence. Additionally, between 1725 EST and 1730 EST, nickel- to quarter-size hail was reported by skywarn observers around Hop Bottom. The general public reported that the hail stripped many local gardens. In Acre Lake an observer reported a driveway was full of hail. No injuries or deaths occurred.
A house sustained an estimated $80,000 worth of fire damage after being struck by lighting.

A small out building was destroyed and the top of a silo was torn off. The front porch collapsed on one house and half the roof was torn off another house and two barns. A few trees were also blown down. The damage to the buildings was almost exclusively located on the south side. All of the debris was blown toward an easterly direction and there was no evidence of any rotation. The damage was caused by a downburst wind estimated to be 60 to 70 knots. An eyewitness said that there was quarter to golfball-size hail between 1740 EST and 1745 EST. An inch or more of hail fell in East Smithfield, followed by 2.00 inches of rain. The hail damaged cornfields and gardens, and on the Berwick Turnpike, a plugged drainage pip funnel a 3-foot pile of hail onto the expressway. One vehicle drove into it. Fortunately, no one was injured.

Numerous trees were downed, and a local resident had a brick and slate chimney blown off of the roof of the house. A large shed was also thrown off its foundation. An investigation by NWS personnel determined that damage was a result of straight line winds.

A lightning stroke apparently knocked down power lines behind the Mountainside Manor Personal Care Home on route 309. The 13,000 volt live power lines sizzled on the wet ground, corning into contact with the back of the building and burning through a section of aluminum siding. No injuries were reported.

June was unusually hot in South Carolina causing record or near record power consumption. Statewide, it was the driest June of record although isolated severe thunderstorms did occur in some sections of the state. The driest part of the state was across the upper piedmont where many areas reported less than 0.25 inch of rain during the month. Some of the smaller monthly amounts were 0.15 inches at Antreville, Abbeville County, 0.17 inches at Greenville-Spartanburg Airport, and 0.20 inches at Nine Islands in Cherokee County. It was the driest June on record in the Greenville-Spartanburg area. Major crop damage was reported statewide with the corn crop particularly hard-hit.
Lightning killed two valuable horses at Rose Hill Plantation.
Some trees were blown down between Lake City and Johnsonville.
Golf ball-size hail occurred.
Thunderstorm wind and lightning caused considerable minor damage in Conway vicinity. Horry Electric Cooperative reported 400 power outages.

A severe thunderstorm moved from Mountain Rest to Walhalla. Falling trees damaged several homes, vehicles, and caused interruptions to power and telephone services.

A severe thunderstorm developed over the western part of Greenville County and moved south through part of the city of Greenville and along the Anderson County border. Trees and power lines were blown down interrupting power for several thousand people in Greenville. Large hail was reported all along the track of the storm before it weakened as it approached the Ware Shoals area.

Persistant heavy rains caused continued flooding of cropland and rivers, including the Big Sioux and Vermillion, in southeast South Dakota, especially in the latter part of the month after the 22nd. In Sioux Falls, both the 6-month and 12-month periods ending June 30th were the wettest on record with about twice the normal precipitation.
Hail fell in the Norbeck Wildlife Refuge between Hill City and Mt. Rushmore.

An earthquake measuring 4.1 on the Richter scale shook a portion of northeast South Dakota but caused no real damage or injuries. The epicenter of the quake was 22 miles northwest of Morris, Minnesota or 38 miles east of Sisseton, South Dakota and was felt in most of Roberts, Grant, and Deuel Counties in northeast South Dakota. The quake was the first in the area since 1975 and it lasted from 4 to 30 seconds. The quake rattled dishes, knocked down some pictures, made lights swing, and otherwise disturbed people and animals.
Three-quarter-inch-diameter hail was reported between Porcupine and Kyle with 0.50-inch hail occurring at Oglala.
Strong Thunderstorm wind damaged several homes.
Over 3.00 inches of rain flooded some basements and gardens, damaged several area roads, and caused a few dams to run over.

One to three inches of rain caused various problems in the Black Hills. At 1343 MDT, a mudslide caused $15,000 in damage to three vehicles in a Keystone parking lot. The slide carried a large pine tree down a hill into the vehicles and also ripped out telephone and electric lines. The heavy rains caused streams to reach bankfull creating some localized flooding problems. Grizzly Gulch Campground near Keystone was temporariliy evacuated. Several roads were closed due to the high waters, mudslides, or debris. Small creeks flooded some basements and threatened homes south of Pactola Reservoir and near Ellsworth Air Force Base causing some residents to be evacuated.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail and heavy rains of up to 3.50 inches inundated an area from northern Clay and Union counties through southeast Turner County to Lincoln County in far southeast South Dakota. The rains caused flooding of basements, roads, and farm fields. In Viborg, 25 homes had up to 2 feet of water in the basements. The downpour also caused urban flooding in Canton shutting down a manufacturing plant.
A boat dock was destroyed by 70-mph winds and resultant waves.

A tornado extensively damaged one farm northeast of Kimball and caused damage to other farms. Several children riding their bicycles in Kimball were picked up by the winds and thrown to the ground causing minor injury.
A tornado ripped out trees and power lines.

A large tornado on the ground for at least 10 minutes destroyed a farmstead. The tornado twisted the house on its foundation virtually destroying it, and destroyed the barn, 3 steel bins, 3 granaries, and 2 hog houses. Ten hogs were also killed. Trees were uprooted and twisted up to a mile north of the farm and pieces of tin roof were wrapped around trees 0.25 mile from the farm.

In the Fedora area and east of Howard the tornadoes destroyed or damaged farm buildings including barns, sheds, and grain bins. East of Howard a tornado also destroyed a feed elevator and tore the roof off a hog plant. Power lines were knocked down and trees uprooted in some areas.

A large tornado and its attendant vortices left a swath of destruction from northwest Minnehaha County through western Moody County into eastern Brookings County. Numerous farms and residences were destroyed or damaged and trees snapped off or uprooted. Around 1630 CDT multiple vortices formed into the tornado two miles west of Lyons destroying barns and silos and killing animals on several farms. Shortly after, the tornado leveled two houses, seriously injuring four people as they were buried in the rubble. It then caused destruction on at least 10 more farms before entering the northwest side of Colman at 1700 CDT. At least 15 homes in Colman had an estimated total of $250,000 in damage mainly due to the roofs either being blown off or trees falling on them. At 1710 CDT the tornado damaged houses and trees three miles north/northeast of Colman. Around 1715 CDT, 10 miles northwest of Flandreau, the tornado leveled a farm, except for the silo, and injured a man who received multiple pelvis fractures. On two farms, one 2 miles southwest of Aurora and the other 1 mile west of Aurora, buildings and grain bins were destroyed around 1735 CDT. The tornado then continued north/northeast, wrecking irrigation systems and uprooting and snapping off hundreds of trees, before causing destruction on another farm about 6 miles northeast of Brookings around 1745 CDT. Northeast of White, three farms sustained major damage to buildings and trees. Cows were also killed and power lines downed.

A large tornado tore a north/northeast path of destruction through at least 10 farms. On one farm southeast of Junius all that remained was the foundation and steps of the house and the bumper and engine of a pickup truck. On other farms livestock were crippled and a horse was impaled by a piece of wood. At least four people were injured as several vehicles were flipped by the tornado. A woman was driving on a highway west of Madison when the wind started spinning her car around and the windows shattered. About 200 power poles were downed leaving 2800 customers without electricity.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple of tornadoes hit farms in the Chester and Wentworth areas. Buildings were damaged or destroyed on farms 2 miles west of Chester, 4 miles northeast of Chester, and north of Wentworth. The tornado blew away an entire residence 2.5 miles north of Wentworth, including the house, garage, and pole shed.

Strong northerly gradient winds buffeted the Black Hills area downing numerous trees loosened by heavy rains the day before. The trees fell on power lines causing power failures throughout the area. A gust to 60 mph was recorded at the Rapid City Airport at 1319 MDT.

Lightning and hail also occurred in the Ft. Pierre and Pierre area with the hail ranging from marble to baseball size.

Dozens of TV's, VCR's, and other electrical devices were blown out by the lightning in the Brookings area. Heavy rains from the storm caused some flooding of county and township roads.

An area extending from Mitchell to Brookings was especially hard hit as flooding affected roads, basements, lakes, creeks, and farmland. Urban flooding occurred in both Mitchell and Brookings. The rain caused Lake Campbell and Lake Hendricks in Brookings County to overflow resulting in some water damage to lakeside homes.

Three of the injuries were caused by trees falling on moving cars, the rest were in damaged homes. By 2050 EDT the last damage was reported in the southeastern corner of the state, just south of Norfolk.

The Great Flood of 1993 along the Mississippi River Valley affected Illinois from East Dubuque
to Cairo. As June ended and July began, the Mississippi River continued to rise. The river was
above flood stage at most locations for the entire month of July. Record crests were reached all
along the Illinois border. Significant flooding also occurred along many of the Illinois tributaries
of the Mississippi, including the lower Rock River, the lower Illinois River, the Big Muddy River
and the Kaskaskia River. The Rock River at Joslin and Moline was still about a foot above flood
stage on the last day of July.
On July 9, the Mississippi River at the Quad Cities reached 22.6 feet. This broke the old record
of 22.5 feet set in 1965. River stage records from 1973 along the Mississippi River from Quincy
south were shattered during this flood. The list below gives some of the records as of 7/31/93.
Since the water was still rising, the final record stages were not reached until August.
Flood Stage Record Date Old Record Date
Quincy Illinois: 17 32.2 7/13/93 28.9 4/73
Grafton, Illinois: 18 37.3 7/31/93 33.1 4/73
Alton, Illinois: 21 41.5 7/31/93 36.6 4/73
Chester, Illinois 27 47.4 7/31/93 43.3 4/73
The flooding put a tremendous strain on many facets of life along and adjacent to the rivers. Not
only were towns and farmland along the rivers affected, but other businesses and people suffered
as well.
Transportation was greatly affected. There are 28 bridges that cross the Mississippi River into Illinois. As of Friday July 16, only 5 were open. The trucking and railroad industries suffered
losses as did people who work on the other side of the river.
Nearly every levee along the Mississippi river, and many along the Illinois river either failed or suffered severe damage. "The cost to repair the levees will go well into the millions.
Barge traffic along the Mississippi was brought to a halt in early July. This meant the loss of an
estimated 1800 jobs and $92 million in revenue a month for the state of Illinois. Total
unemployment in Illinois due to the flood was estimated at 9,000. People of all walks of life came
to the area to help fight the flood. Over 4500 Illinois National Guard Troops were called to duty
to provide security, patrol levees, operate pumps, move materials and fill sandbags. About 400
medium security inmates from various prisons also helped with the sandbagging.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front began moving into Iowa from the northwest. Copious amounts of moisture was available for this event with precipitable water values around two inches. Thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon hours. By the early evening the storms had formed into a well developed mesoscale convective system. The main feature with the storms was the heavy rainfall, however there was some severe weather associated with the storms during the event. Golf ball-size hail pelted the area around Schleswig in Crawford County. In fact, baseball-size hail to the south of Schleswig caused total crop destruction in the area. The largest hail reported was in Harrison County at Little Sioux. Hail reached three inches in diameter causing considerable crop damage. In Dow City, also in Crawford County, high winds in what appeared to be a microburst struck. A farm was leveled by winds around 85 MPH. High winds were also reported in Carroll County in the city of Carroll. Minor damage occurred in Decatur City in Decatur County during the decaying stages of the system. There were a few tornadoes spawned by the system. They were each quite small and were only on the ground for a short period of time. One tornado touched down in Crawford County south of Vail. The tornado downed several trees and destroyed a few out buildings. Another tornado touched down near Boone in an open field, causing little damage. A similar situation occurred in Greene County west of Jefferson as well as in Chickasaw County north of New Hampton. One of the storms became rather intense and produced a tornado that was on the ground in Dallas County for several miles. Little damage was reported as the tornado passed between several farmsteads. The same storm cluster later produced a funnel cloud over the northeast part of Des Moines. Reports indicated the funnel was very near touching the ground. Other reports of funnel clouds were received from Cherokee County, where four of them were observed west of Cherokee. A few funnel cloud reports were also received from the surrounding counties, but there were no touch downs. Extremely heavy rainfall was reported in Audubon, Crawford, Carroll, and Greene Counties. Damage was very heavy in Crawford County. Initial reports showed that damage in the county was in the $3-4 million range. Story County was also hard hit as 2 1/2 to 5 inches of rain fell across the Squaw Creek basin. Flooding was severe in Ames, with the creek reaching an all time high. Damage to Iowa State University was in the millions of dollars. The Skunk River also rose markedly, causing additional problems, and eventually closing Interstate 35 fora while. The heaviest rainfall was reported around Coon Rapids with 7.83 inches falling in a few hours time. There were numerous reports of three to seven inch rainfall amounts. Manilla reported 7.50 inches of rainfall, with nearly that amount in Denison. Unofficial amounts were higher. In Greene County, the city of Scranton reported 11 inches of rainfall, while ten inches was reported in Carroll County at Willey. In Crawford County, damage from flash flooding was estimated at $15 million. Severe flood damage occurred in 50 homes in Denison and 36 in Dow City. The water rose so quickly that reports indicated that some homes flooded in as little at 11 minutes. Monona County was also hard hit, with rainfall in the four to nine inch range from Onawa east into Harrison County. Damage was extensive in Shelby County where the flood waters washed out several bridges. Highway 59 was under water two miles south of Defiance. Highway 191 was closed between Earling and Panama by flooding from Mosquito Creek. Two hundred and fifty people were forced out of a mobile home park in Harlan, where the water and sewage plant was flooded. Water ran three feet deep in Irwin. Heavy rainfall in excess of three inches fell across much of the north half of the Raccoon River Basin, and extended into the middle Des Moines River Basin. These rains closed numerous roads and washed out bridges in several counties. At one time the Crawford County sheriff reported that nearly all roads in the county were closed by high water. The heavy rainfall set the stage for what was to become the flood of record along the Raccoon and Des Moines River. Flash flooding also occurred east of this area along much of the line of thunderstorms. The flooding extended on a scattered basis all the way to the northeast part of the state. Some of the heavier rains fell in Tama County. Four inches of rain fell resulting in water in the streets of Tama and Chelsea of seven feet in depth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Southern Iowa was ahead of the cold front in the warm sector. During the evening hours a Derecho formed over southern Nebraska. The Derecho races across southern Nebraska and southern Iowa at 50 to 60 knots. High winds in the 70 to 100 MPH range were reported with the system. As the storms moved into Iowa, a Bow Echo formed on the lead edge. High winds of 90 to 100 MPH downed 13 high tension power line poles in the eastern part of Council Bluffs. Winds of at least 85 MPH ripped into Fremont County, blowing a church off of its foundation in Bartlett. Considerable tree and building structural damage was reported across the southwest quarter of the state. As an example, roof damage was reported to one house and garage with windows blown in at Pilot Grove Park in Montgomery County, with a shed and barn leveled in Page County near Bethesda. There were two injuries as the storms rolled through. One was south of Glenwood in Mills County as a woman sustained minor injuries from flying debris. Another woman was cut by flying glass near Portsmouth as high winds ripped through the area. Other damage in southwest Iowa included the roof being blown off of a house south of Glenwood and another roof taken off of a mobile home hear Hastings. High winds uprooted trees in Red Oak in Montgomery County. Five miles east of Elliot, a house had windows blown out and damage was done to the roof. As the storms moved into Des Moines, high winds blew car windows out on the south side of the city. High winds in Warren county picked up a gravity bin wagon north of Lacona and threw it 50 feet. A pontoon boat was tossed 100 feet by high winds near Seymour. A few tornadoes were reported. One was actually a gustnado in Monroe County. Several roofs were damaged and tree tops were taken off in the town of Albia. Another tornado touched down briefly north of Agency in Wapello County. A metal building was completely flattened. In what turned out to be one of the stronger tornadoes, a touchdown was reported in the Portsmouth area. Two houses were damaged extensively. In addition, a mobile home was overturned with the roof taken off of another building. A horse trailer was picked up and carried for 250 feet. Rainfall was heavy with the Derecho, but with the speed of movement the amounts were generally less than an inch. Late in the severe weather episode, general river flooding began. The Boyer River flooded through Harrison County from heavy upstream rains. Homes, businesses, and croplands were flooded including areas around Woodbine and Missouri Valley. Seventy five to 80 homes were flooded in Missouri Valley where water was 3 to 4 feet deep in places. The Missouri River also flooded the Willow Creek Area. The West Nishnabotna River flooded through Pottawattamie County. About 50 people were evacuated in Avoca where water flooded the town to the highest levels since 1947. Interstate 80 was closed in the area for a time on the 9th after water swept a number of cars off the roadway. Downstream, record flooding occurred around the Hancock area where the park was heavily damaged. The crest rolled into the Oakland area early on the 10th, overflowing sand bags and flooding widespread areas of the town. Numerous roads were flooded and bridges damaged. Crop damage was heavy. The Missouri River also overflowed, forcing evacuations at Goose Haven and Honey Creek. In Mills and Fremont Counties, the West Nishnabotna River flooded croplands and roads throughout the area, damaging some bridges. Some overflows affected the area around Hastings.

The heavy rainfall event that occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 8th into the early morning of the 9th set the stage for what was to become the flood of the century, or the great floo?
of 1993. Several events took place to cause the major flooding to occur. Heavy rainfall, as much
as 11 inches in places, occurred during the afternoon and evening hours of the 8th. The heaviest
rainfall fell along the upper reaches of the Raccoon River. Heavy rainfall of several inches was reported over almost all of the state during this period. By the afternoon of the 9th, the lake levels
at Lake Panora had risen so rapidly a decision was made to release over three hundred million cubic
feet of water from the lake in a rush that local residents said sounded like the dam had broken.
Another round of rainfall occurred on the morning of the 10th across northern Iowa, adding to an already serious situation. By the 10th, record crests were moving down many of lowa's rivers.
In what added the crowning glory to the flooding, heavy rainfall of two to three inches, with isolated amounts between four and five inches, fell over western and central Iowa at the time the
crest was approaching the area. Record river levels were recorded in many areas. For example,
the Raccoon River crested near seven feet over the all time record crest at the southwest 18th street
bridge. The Des Moines Water Treatment plant on Fleur Drive was inundated by water during the
predawn hours of the 11th. This resulted in the loss of water for 250,000 residents for 12 days,
and stopped the flow of drinking water for 19 days. Water service was lost to many communities
around the state during this period of extreme flooding. Damage around the state was extensive and
well into the billions of dollars. Within a few days of the floods beginning all 99 counties in Iowa
had received the federal disaster declaration. In addition to the record crests on the rivers,
reservoirs around the state reached record levels. Saylorville Reservoir overflowed for the second
time in 1993 and crested around 56 feet over normal pool state. Coralville Reservoir overflowed
for the first time in its history as did Red Rock Reservoir. Rathbun Reservoir overflowed late in
the month. The total dollar damage estimates were nowhere close to being in by the time of this writing. A few estimates had been received on a preliminary basis. The city of Des Moines was
hard hit. At the peak of the flooding, between 30,000 and 35,000 households were without electricity and 50,000 were without power at one time or another during the flood. Water service
was out for 250,000 people, which as mentioned was the largest water outage in United States
history. Losses to the business in the area due to lost business were estimated at $700,000,000.
Other damage in Des Moines included $253 million in physical damage, $30 million in damage to
homes, $100 million in damages to businesses, $75 million to the levee system, and $20 million damage to the water treatment plant. Reports from West Des Moines included 237 businesses
damaged at a cost of $20 million, 685 homes damaged at a cost of $6 million, damage to the streets
and sanitary system was $6 million, and $3 million in damages to city parks. Some examples of damages to more rural areas: In Des Moines County, 250 houses were damaged, 50 businesses damaged, and eight municipal buildings damaged. In Van Buren County damages were estimated around $5 million. Damage occurred to 165 homes and ten mobile homes. Thirteens homes were destroyed. Eighty one businesses were damaged, three of which were destroyed. Thirty four miles
of roads were severely damaged. Four hundred homes had to be evacuated. There were two flood
related injuries in Van Buren County as a couple was trapped in their basement by the rising water.
The husband sustained a broken arm, his wife sustained superficial wounds. Reports like these
were filed for nearly every county in the state. A complete report is beyond the scope of this
report. There were four people hospitalized in lowa City as bacteria crept into the water supply. The flooding was extensive with hundreds of roads closed around the state. Many of the interstates
were closed at times as well. Interstate 380 was closed as the water from the Coralville Reservoir
overtopped the roadway. Interstate 80 was closed by the Raccoon, Des Moines, and Skunk Rivers.
Interstate 35 was closed by the Skunk and Raccoon Rivers. Crop damage was extensive as well.
Many areas were under water for extended periods of time, destroying crops. Reports indicated
that 6.5 million acres of cropland were damaged by this flood alone.

In Mills and Fremont Counties, the West Nishnabotna River flooded croplands and roads throughout the area, damaging some bridges.

The storms fired during the early afternoon hours. They tracked across northern Iowa into the east-central counties. A few tornadoes were spawned by the stronger storms. One touched down briefly in Cerro Gordo County. The second touched down in Floyd County. This tornado was on the ground for about 12 mifes and caused damage to a few farmsteads. For the most part the storms caused high winds, at times gusting to around 80 MPH. Winds gusted to 80 MPH in Ogden, in Boone County. Numerous reports of trees and power lines being downed by the high winds were received. Early in the storms development, large hail was reported in northwest Iowa. Baseball and larger size hail fell in Lyon and Sioux Counties with a swath of 90% crop damage from northwest to southeast of Boydon. All of the windows on the north side of the houses in Boydon were broken by the hail. Other reports of hail were received after these initial reports. Most of the hail was pea to marble-size. Three-quarter inch diameter hail fell in Winneshiek County at Decorah, while the largest hail report was in Webster County. Callender reported golf ball to softball-size hail briefly. Crops were destroyed and leaves stripped off of trees in the area. The combination of the hail and three inches of rainfall caused large drifts of hail. High winds resulted in an injury in Floyd County. An 11 year old was injured at a campground as a tree branch fell on his leg. In Palo Alto County, lightning struck a golf cart shed at a local golf course. It started a fire that destroyed the shed and several carts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The synoptic situation was set up a little differently than that of the past several days. The warm front had moved north into Iowa, however several old outflow boundaries remained from the past days convection. There were three main differences in the pattern on this day as compared with the previous several. The first was that a strong low level jet became established during the evening. What was on the order of 30 kts by late afternoon increased to 50 to 60 kts during the evening. This was stronger than the low level jet of the past several days. A cold front was approaching, which also aided in the formation of convection. The third factor was a strong short wave, or upper air disturbance, approaching the area. These factors combined to set of explosive thunderstorm development during the late afternoon hours into the evening. The storms first fired up over southeast Nebraska. The storm cluster expanded into a mesoscale convective complex in just three hours time as the low level jet pushed a pool of 75 to 80 degree dew point temperatures into the region. The storms produced copious rainfall over parts of Nebraska. During the early evening a strong line developed on the lead edge of the complex. This line advanced into lowa at nearly 50 kts. This spared lowa of what could have been a flooding/flash flooding event of historical proportions. The speed of movement kept precipitation amounts under two inches in most areas. Heavy rainfall of two inches in a 30 minute time me period was reported in Council Bluffs area. Streets were flooded with numerous intersections under water. A theater was damaged when flood waters crept in. About two feet of water covered the theater's parking lot. The storm complex was tornadic as it moved across southeast Nebraska. Two tornadoes were spawned in southwest Iowa. The first straddled the Mills and Fremont County line south of Glenwood. It was preceded by two funnel cloud reports in Fremont County about 20 minutes prior to touchdown. The tornado damaged trees and caused considerable damage to a mobile home east of Bartlett. The main feature with the storms was high winds. A few funnel clouds were reported over southwest Iowa during the early stages of the event. They were reported in both Page and Adams Counties. A small tornado touched down briefly in the town of Corning about an hour before. The funnel cloud came from a secondary storm that developed. The storms did produce some small hail in the Moville area of Woodbury County. Reports of winds of 70 MPH or more were numerous. Tree and power line damage was quite widespread. In Woodbury County northwest of Climbing Hill, high winds downed power lines and damaged a hog shed on one farm. Sheet metal was strewn across the road there. High winds struck southeast of the town of Treynor in Pottawattamie County. The 75 MPH winds downed several barns and damaged outbuildings in the area. Two farms south of Walnut sustained heavy damage from the thunderstorm winds. A roof was lifted off one farmhouse. A large metal storage shed was twisted and smashed. A barn was destroyed and several grain bins were lifted. The storms high winds downed a barn south of Creston, in Union County. Considerable damage was reported in Guthrie County. A lot of trees were downed, the roof was taken off of one house, part of the roof on the 4H building, and the roof of the ready mix plant were all taken off in Guthrie Center. A small camper was moved across a parking lot there as well. Needless to say, considerable damage was also done to power lines in the area. As one of the stronger storms moved across the Des Moines Airport, very high winds were recorded. An apparent microburst occurred along with the passage of the gust front. In actuality, the highest winds occurred after the first thunderstorms moved over the airport. An intense storm just to the south of the airport resulted in wind gusts of 83 MPH at the airport. The Air Traffic Control Tower recorded a sustained 89 MPH wind for a period of several minutes. The storms moved east and produced 70 MPH winds in northern Warren County at Carlisle. Significant tree and power line damage was reported in the area. Another isolated wind event occurred in Franklin County at Hampton. Roof damage was reported from several buildings at the Franklin County Fairgrounds, caused by high winds. After midnight, a small cluster of storms formed in southwest Iowa. They became severe and produced high winds in Union County in the Creston area. The area southwest of Creston was hardest hit when high winds leveled a block wide area. Once again, this appeared to be a microburst and not a tornado in spite of the fact that the radar echo tops were in excess of 70,000 feet. The storm continued to move east and produced high winds in Clarke County. Winds downed several trees and some power lines in Osceola. All of the storms produced torrential rains. Flash flooding was minimal due to the speed of movement, however there were some local problems mainly in urban areas. The storms moved east during the night and resulted in damage as they moved through Cedar County. An outbuilding was moved off of its foundation west of Lowden. North of Lowden, shingles were blown off of a house and stuck into the screen in front of a picture window. Several trees were downed in the area as well.

Heavy rainfall that began in late June became more persistent and widespread during July causing severe, significant and in some areas record setting flooding. Rainfall amounts during July of 8 to 18 inches were common with some areas along the Nebraska border picking up 20 to 24 inches. Most rainfall fell during the first three weeks of the month and ended in many areas by the 27th. The rainfall coupled with saturated soil and eventually large discharges from completely filled Corp of Engineers reservoirs produced flooding along every river, stream and creek across the area. Even on days when rains did not occur rivers remained in flood or very high as water flowed into them from the swollen lakes and reservoirs. Scattered thunderstorms produced areas of flash flooding during the month especially from July 17th to the 25th. The Flood of '93 as it was called was compared to the record setting Flood of 1951 both in areas covered and magnitude. However, due to flood control levees and reservoirs, flooding in 1993 was not as damaging nor deadly. Flooded farmland was eastimated at 75,000 to 100,000 acres. The Kansas River at Topeka crested at 34.8 ft, the highest in 20 years, at Manhattan at 30.0 ft, while the Big Blue River at Blue Rapids crested at a record 63.1 ft nearly 40 ft above flood stage. Property and crop damage only in northeast Kansas was estimated at $30 to $40 million.

This event actually began in June and continued through July 31. The flooding that began in the latter half of June continued into July as heavy precipitation coninued and runoff increased. As these heavy rains continued, virtually every low lying or flood prone area had begun to fill with water and persons flying over the area said that the whole region looked more like a giant lake. Floodwaters continued to rise, more homes and businesses had to be evacuated and more roads and bridges had to be closed from either being washed away or flooded. In almost all areas, water levels were at an all time high and there seemed to be no end in sight. Several major reservoirs got so full that in spite of the effects on the ongoing flood situation, water had to be released for fear of dam breakage. By the third week in July, the heavy rains had subsided, but due to the backwaters and excessive flooding downstream, water levels did not drop below flood stage until the 31st.

The combination of runoff from thunderstorms over the upper reaches of the Missouri River basin and repeated heavy rains over the local region, sent the Missouri and Kansas Rivers to historic heights. Record crests were set at most locations along the Missouri River, including Atchison, Kansas (est 30.7 ft on 7/15/93). Many of the sites set records during the of the month, and then reset even higher crests towards month's end. The Kansas River also spent much of the month well above flood stage, being heavily influenced by record crests on the Missouri River. The river crested at De Soto at 26.97 ft on 7/28/93 while at Kansas City it crested at 54.97 ft on 7/28/93. Approximately 60,000 acres of crops were affected by the flooding in Doniphan, Johnson, Leavenworth and Wyandotte counties. The Missouri flooding forced more than 1000 people to evacuate in Elwood, Kansas where a levee was topped. Fifteen hundred people were flooded out of their homes in Wyandotte County, and another 3500 families were evacuated as a precautionary measure from an area where the Kansas and Missouri Rivers converge in Kansas City, Kansas. Damage to roads, bridges, and homes along the flooded rivers were estimated at nearly $10 million throughout the 4 county area. The event lasted all month with waters finally falling below flood stage in early August.

This event began around 2000 CST on 7/1/93 and continued through 7/31/93. As the heavy rain pattern began to spread across the Western portions of Central Kansas during the last week of June, the ground became saturated and the area creeks, rivers, and tributaries were on the rise. During the evening of July 1, three to six inch rainfalls were reported across portions of this area caused massive flooding to begin. From this point on, heavy rainfalls continued on a fairly regular basis which kept water at record high levels. In addition to the rainfall, water continued to back into this area due to the excessive flooding downstream. This combination kept water levels at or above flood stage the entire month. Like the flooding across the rest of Central and North Central Kansas, numerous homes and businesses had to be evacuated as severe and extensive damage was being inflicted upon buildings, roadways, and farmsland. Numerous roads and bridges had to be closed and many fields were so full of water they looked like shallow lakes. The heavy rains began to let up in the third week of July, but due to the excessive flooding elsewhere and the backwaters associated with it, water levels did not drop below flood stage until the 31st.

A tornado touched down on the north side of Mackinac Island. The tornado path was from British Landing on the northwest side of the island northeast to the other side of the island near Scotts Shore road. Ground survey indicated trees in some areas had fallen down in different directions. Some trees were also uprooted.

The path extended from 3/4 mile south of British Landing to 1/4 mile south of British Landing. Some trees were uprooted and some were broken and twisted along the path. Buildings in this area has some damage to roofs due to fallen trees. Trees up to 25 inches in diameter were destroyed. Only about 10 percent of the path had destruction. One minor injury was reported from flying glass due to the wind. Power was out in the affected areas for 14 to 16 hours.

The rainfall for July was much above normal for all of North Dakota. Monthly amounts ranged from five to ten inches over most of the state. However, the National Weather Service Office in Bismarck recorded 13.75 inches of rain, an all-time monthly record. In the town of Wilton, 20 miles north of Bismarck, 16.81 inches of rain fell during the month. The heavy rains caused major urban flooding in the cities of Bismarck, Mandan, Jamestown, Valley City, Devils Lake, Grafton and and Fargo. Small towns, such as Glen Ullin and Fessenden, and rural communities were also affected. Many rivers and streams reached record high stages. Total damage was over $406,000, mostly to crops, and many farmers were unable to plant their flooded fields. Many highways, roads and railroad tracks were washed out. On July 21, Governor Ed Schafer declared the entire state a disaster area, due to the worst flooding ever. The excessive rains, cloudy skies, and cool weather, hurt tourism and outdoor recreation.

A massive thunderstorm complex moved east-southeast across much of northeast Ohio. Widespread tree and roof damage occurred as peak winds were estimated to 100 mph. Hardest hit areas were northeast Cuyahoga, western Lake and much of Geauga County where a series of downbursts downed thousands of trees, many on structures and cars. Several large buildings lost all or a large part of their roof including Municipal Stadium in downtown Cleveland, Willoughby South High School gym and Middlefield Plastics. Winds were measured at 92 mph at Cuyahoga County Airport and at 93 mph at Novelty. A local man was killed in Mesopotamia when a large tree limb impaled him in the drivers seat of his car. A Willowick man died after touching a downed live electric wire. Two men, one from Cuyahoga and one from Lake County died during the clean-up effort from tree-cutting accidents. Most injuries were due to falling trees, flying debris, and breaking glass. State of emegrgencies were declared in Cuyahoga, Lake, and Geauga Counties and some communities were without electricity for seven days. Damage estimate $25 million.

A persistent ridge of high pressure centered over the southeast and extending northward well into the Middle Atlantic region began a heat wave that lasted eleven days. The searing daytime heat, followed by humid nights offering no relief, resulted in numerous deaths-- especially in Philadelphia. This heat wave claimed over one hundred lives in Philadelphia /107/, most of which apparently occurred over the weekend of the 9th and 10th. The number of deaths related to this heat wave was the most ever in Philadelphia, however, this number was highly controversial and partially a result of a campaign to educate the public about preventable deaths among the frail elderly. The overwhelming majority of the deaths were among people 60 years and older. In too many cases, the victims had been shuttered away in the upstairs of intercity apartments with no fan or air conditioner. In Philadelphia, there were nine days of 95 or above temperatures during the heat wave. July 2nd to July 4th marked three consecutive days with a temperatures of 100 degrees or more. Aside from the fatalities related to the excessive heat, several concrete roads buckled and/or exploded, crops were scorched, and livestock were less productive. The actual extent of damage is difficult (if not impossible) to estimate.

BEGIN_LOCATION: Aurora, Davison, Hanson, McCook, Lake, Moody, NW Minnehaha, southern Brookings, SE Miner counties
EVENT_NARRATIVE:
Flash flooding resulted from very heavy thunderstorms which moved from Aurora county east/northeast to Moody county in southeast South Dakota. Three to six inches of rain occurred in
a two to four hour period over already saturated ground. Cities, roads, farms, and lakefront areas
received water damage from the flooding. Some of the cities and towns hardest hit were Madison,
Mt. Vernon, Montrose, and Mitchell. In Aurora and Davison counties, a 12 mile stretch of
Interstate 90 was closed between Plankinton and Mt. Vernon due to water running over the highway. Three inches of rain in Stickney caused some flooding of sewers and basements. In Mt.
Vernon at least five inches resulted in two to three feet of water running down the main street.
About 90 percent of homes and businesses in the town were affected by the flooding, and in one
home a wall caved in. Up to 500 volunteers used at least 12,000 sand bags in Mt. Vernon and near
Dry Run Creek in Mitchell to try to prevent flood damage. Nearly all of a golf course near Dry
Run and Firesteel Creeks was submerged causing severe damage. Many basements were flooded
in Mitchell. At least seven bridges were washed out in Hanson and MeCook counties and many
more were damaged or under water. Many county and township roads were washed out. Damages
to roads and bridges from the flooding were later estimated to be near $500,000 in Hanson county
and $600,000 in Moody county. In McCook county around 0800 CST a man had to be rescued by
boat from the top of his pickup truck which was nearly submerged in water. The truck was swept
off the road by torrents of water north of Salem. Water covered fields and pastures for mile after
mile in northern McCook county, southeast Miner county, and Lake county where four to six inches of rain occurred. In Miner county, water covered much of Canova and flooded basements in
Howard. In Lake county, major flash flooding hit the city of Madison where over five inches of
rain caused Lake Herman, Memorial Creek, and Silver Creek to overflow. Especially hard hit was
the south side of Madison where Silver Creek connects Lake Herman to the west from Lake
Madison to the east. Two thousand residents and a nursing home were evacuated. About 500
homes had some degree of water damage. It was estimated there were 18 basement cave-ins.
Numerous homes and businesses had several feet of water in them. At least 50 people were brought
out of their homes by boat and some had to be rescued as the water rose very quickly. One person
was swept away by the current but eventually got hold of a fence. Two other people had to hang
on to a tree to save themselves. Two rescue workers received minor injuries trying to help people
out of their homes. At the Madison wastewater treatment plant 250 feet of main sewer line gave
way, the motors were flooded, and a bridge near the plant was torn out. Homes and some
businesses around Lake Herman, Lake Madison, and Lake Brant also sustained flood damage as
the lakes reached record high levels. Water covered some homes to the roof level near Lake
Madison. Many roads, culverts, and bridges in the affected counties were undermined. Major
flooding affected area lakes, creeks, and rivers including the Big Sioux River and Vermillion River
through the night of July 3rd and the next few days. Especially hard hit was Montrose near the east
Vermillion River and Lake Campbell in southern Brookings county. In Montrose where floodwaters
hit their peak about 2300 CST July 3rd, 52 families were evacuated and at least ten families lost
their homes. The Montrose sewage treatment plant was flooded and a river of water ran through
the Montrose grain elevator and the main street. Water was one foot from going over the top of
the Lake Vermillion dam downstream of Montrose at 1900 CST July 4th before the flood gates were opened. At Lake Campbell, where the flood levels were the highest ever remembered,
residents were forced out ofa dozen homes. The flooding took out long distance phone service for
many areas. The main fiber optic cable that serves eastern South Dakota was washed away south
of Lake Vermillion. Other cities later affected by the flooding on the Vermillion River included
Davis and Centerville. Flooding affected communities along the Big Sioux River including Flandreau, Egan, Trent, Dell Rapids, Baltic, and Renner. A man died July 4th when his car was
swept away around 1230 CST while he tried to drive on a closed and flooded road one mile east
of Dell Rapids near the Big Sioux River. (M82V)

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three to nine inches of rain caused widespread flash flooding and flood damage. Especially hard hit was an area from Webster northeastward through the Pickerell and Buffalo Lakes area to Sisseton where the situation was declared a state of emergency and ultimately a disaster area. The heavy rains overwhelmed a small creek that flows through Sisseton, swelling it to three blocks wide and up to five feet deep by 1930 CST. The rushing waters carried lumber, railroad ties, propane tanks, and several vehicles. Flood damage occurred to 70 percent of all buildings in Sisseton, including 100 homes, 15 of which were evacuated, and at least six businesses. In one home the floor caved in and in another the flash flood went right through the home. Two city streets also caved in. In Webster, the excessive rain flooded all the sewer lifts that pump water out of low-lying areas in town. The sewer system then backed up into homes and businesses. Nine of the 12 main floor rooms at the Super 8 motel in Webster were flooded by the rainstorm and some people had to be moved from their rooms. Road and bridge damage was also extensive in Roberts, Day, and Marshall counties with about 50 roads and bridges in Day county damaged by the flooding. Area lakes including Pickerell, Blue Dog, Enemy Swim, and Buffalo lakes rose over two feet, inundating areas around lake homes, submerging docks, and setting boats adrift. Other areas had up to three feet of water over roads including state highway 10 between Sisseton and Lake City. Many basements and buildings were flooded.

One of the driest July's on record prevailed over north Texas in 1993. At many locations (including Fort Worth and Waco),no rain was reported in July for the first time since records began (going back nearly a hundred years). By the end of the month,many crops were reported suffering from the lack of rain. Brush and grass fires were increasing in frequency,including one that burned 4000 acres of ranch land in Young county and another that burned 2800 acres in Palo Pinto county. The Texas Forest Service declared the eastern two-thirds of the state (some 50 million acres) was in extreme fire danger,and by the end of month,many counties had banned outdoor burning. Water supply was only a problem in a few rural areas,as most lakes and reservoirs were full from spring rains. Monthly rainfall of 4 to over 14 inches over southern and central Wisconsin continued the flooding problems of the previous month. The Mississippi River,at least seven major rivers,many smaller streams and tributaries,and numerous lakes overflowed their banks during the month. The Pecatonica River basin in south-central Wisconsin received the brunt of the rainfall and worst flooding. A record flood occurred at Blanchardville (Lafayette County) with near record flooding at Darlington (Lafayette County) and Martintown (Green County). The Fox River near Berlin (Green Lake County) and Pecatonica River at Martintown remained above flood stage all month. Much of downtown Darlington was flooded along with parts of Blanchardville as the Pecatonica crested on July 6th. Damage resulting from the widespread flooding was mainly in crop losses. Since the rain and flooding began in the spring,crop and infrastructure damage estimates by county included Jackson $50 million,Lafayette $10.5 million,Adams $10 million,Juneau $9 million,Green $7 million,Waupaca $6 million and Columbia $4 million. By the end of July,39 counties were declared federal disaster areas. Overall damage this agricultural season affected 2.25 million acres,totalling $525 million,with $450 million from flooding and excessive rains,and $125 million from winter-kill of 750,000 acres of alfalfa. Over 56,000 farmers were affected by these weather conditions. When losses from reduced yields are added,the estimated total crop loss would be near $1 billion. The flooding continued to affect tourism,outdoor activities,construction and sporting events.

By the end of July,39 counties were declared federal disaster areas. Overall damage this agricultural season affected 2.25 million acres,totalling $525 million,with $450 million from flooding and excessive rains,and $125 million from winter-kill of 750,000 acres of alfalfa. Over 56,000 farmers were affected by these weather conditions. When losses from reduced yields are added,the estimated total crop loss would be near $1 billion. The flooding continued to affect tourism,outdoor activities,construction and sporting events.
An isolated severe thunderstorm knocked down power lines and trees, some of which damaged homes near Spread Eagle (Florence County).

A line of severe thunderstorms containing hail up to three-quarters inch in diameter and packing high winds hit portions of northeast and south-central Wisconsin. Intense winds toppled trees which damaged four mobile homes east of Evansville (Rock County). Winds also leveled a tobacco shed, hog house and trees south of Fulton (Rock County). Heavy rain caused Badfish Creek to overflow its banks flooding 15 homes and causing $130,000 in damage in Oregon (Dane County).

A line of severe thunderstorms swept across southern Wisconsin accompanied by one tornado, winds gusting up to 70 mph and hail up to nickel-size. Three golfers were injured when struck by a lightning bolt near Holmen (LaCrosse County). A tornado briefly set down near the northeast shore of Lake Eau Claire (Eau Claire County) and damaged 12 trees. Violent Thunderstorm wind pushed a mobile home off its foundation near Cataract (Monroe County), damaged 12 homes and five cars in Sun Prairie (Dane County) and caused a variety of damage to 13 planes and a small building at the EAA Fly-In at Oshkosh (Winnebago County). Otherwise damage was confined to trees and power lines.
